attempts.answer:
Below is a structured literature review on the feasibility of Bring‑Your‑Own‑Device (BYOD) for large, high‑stakes university exams, drawing on case studies, comparative experiments, and feasibility/policy analyses. We synthesize “success stories” with student counts, outline operational models (BYOD vs rental devices vs dedicated labs/remote proctoring), and weigh integrity, cost, and logistics.

Key takeaways at a glance
- BYOD is feasible at scale for high‑stakes exams when institutions address connectivity, device parity, proctoring, and fairness with a secure exam platform and clear policies; large‑class implementations report both satisfaction and actionable limitations, and dedicated exam centers can be prohibitively expensive, pushing institutions toward BYOD as an economically viable option where throughput and cost are critical constraints. <cite id="09e14b96-0">One common thread that runs through the areas for improvement is related to the exam venue, which ideally could be solved with a dedicated exam centre that is equipped with wired internet connected computers and that is large enough to accommodate a large class; however, the cost of setting-up and running such an exam centre remains a major roadblock, making BYOD e-exams a potentially only feasible and economically-viable option</cite> <cite id="09e14b96-4">A bring-your-own-laptop high-stakes open-book final examination for a General Biology course with an enrolment of 672 students was held at the National University of Singapore, with pre/post surveys and focus groups identifying satisfaction and areas for improvement</cite> <cite id="09e14b96-1">Institutions cannot afford to invest in fleets of computers reserved solely for semi-annual testing, making BYOD critical while bringing challenges of validity and reliability</cite>.

Feasibility conditions and constraints
- Connectivity and device parity: BYOD implementations are sensitive to venue Wi‑Fi reliability, device diversity (Windows/macOS/tablets), and uneven hardware capabilities; these issues can be mitigated by reserving wired‑connected, centrally managed lab workstations for fallback, but upfront capex and running costs can be significant, nudging institutions toward BYOD when capacity and cost dominate. <cite id="09e14b96-0">Exam venue limitations and connectivity quality were recurrent pain points; wired, dedicated exam centers improve limitations but are costly, making BYOD more attractive on cost grounds</cite> <cite id="6c95020f-2">Modern teaching increasingly uses students' personal devices; diversity of software and platforms and information security challenges hinder implementation</cite>.
- Security/integrity: BYOD raises cheating risks unless the exam platform enforces lockdown, restricts OS/app access, and supports identity verification and remote invigilation; evidence shows measurable impact on fairness and detectability of anomalies when these controls are absent or weak. <cite id="05b2a8df-3">Allowing students to bring their own device poses cheating-related issues; lockdown browsers and automated video proctoring are common approaches to create secure workstations and monitor exams</cite> <cite id="6c95020f-0">Remote invigilation uses webcams, screen recording, and AI analytics to detect anomalies such as unauthorized device usage or multiple individuals in a candidate's exam space, but raises privacy and technical disruption concerns</cite>.
- Accessibility and policy: BYOD requires clear EULAs/consent for camera/microphone use, accommodations for disability/accessibility, and processes to support a wide range of assistive technologies; fairness concerns motivate platforms that standardize the candidate environment. <cite id="05b2a8df-3">Security approaches include lockdown browsers and crash-recovery modes; specialized tools restrict unauthorized access and randomize questions to reduce advantage</cite> <cite id="6c95020f-0">AI-enabled systems flag suspicious activities, but institutions must implement clear policies around data security and privacy to maintain trust</cite>.

Success stories and scale
- National University of Singapore (NUS), large class feasibility: <cite id="09e14b96-4">In November 2013, NUS ran a BYOD high‑stakes open‑book final exam for 672 students, collecting pre/post surveys and focus groups; results showed both satisfaction and surfaced areas for improvement (e.g., connectivity, instructions, device readiness), and the paper details implementation and limitations</cite>. 
- Monash College (Australia), pre‑university to university pathway: <cite id="09e14b96-2">Trials of supervised short‑text and essay responses using BYOD in two units of the Foundation Year programme (Monash College) explored authentic e‑assessment in exam rooms, supported by a national Australian government‑funded grant investigating BYOD in university examinations</cite>.
- Empirical feedback at scale: <cite id="09e14b96-3">An institutional study invited all 920 students who took BYOD final exams to complete a survey (51% response); items covered device hardware/software, experience with computer‑based exams, perceptions of cheating, preferred exam location, adequacy of lecture‑hall infrastructure, and advantages/disadvantages, yielding actionable insights for continuous improvement</cite>.
- Australia’s “Transforming Exams” national initiative: <cite id="09e14b96-1">Australia is undergoing a cultural and technical shift for high‑stakes assessment; BYOD is positioned as critical to meet capacity without fleets of dedicated test computers, while acknowledging validity and reliability challenges that projects like Transforming Exams aim to address</cite>.

Comparative modes: BYOD vs. rental devices vs. dedicated labs/remote proctoring
Operational models and throughput
- BYOD: Pros and cons. Pros include zero upfront device capex, high throughput because students already own devices, and flexibility to run hybrid (on‑campus and remote) invigilation; cons include heterogeneity, connectivity variability, and integrity risks unless mitigated with secure platforms and proctoring. <cite id="09e14b96-0">BYOD addresses capacity but venue/connectivity issues persist; dedicated exam halls reduce limitations but are costly</cite> <cite id="05b2a8df-3">Lockdown browsers and secure frameworks can transform personal devices into controlled workstations; platforms like Safe Exam Browser restrict access and support crash recovery</cite>.
- Rental/loaner device programs: Institutions often supplement BYOD with hourly/fee loaner devices for students without personal devices; this balances equity and cost but adds logistics (turnaround, sanitization, technical support). <cite id="6c95020f-4">Universities run loan programs where students borrow university-owned laptops by the hour; deposits and program changes affect uptake, and device diversity and affordability motivate mixed strategies</cite> <cite id="6c95020f-2">Students’ devices are extremely diverse; universities canceled a one‑to‑one laptop program and observed a fall in classroom laptop use, reinforcing the need for flexible access and clear BYOD strategies</cite>. Evidence gaps: published, quantitative failure rates and cost per device for university exam‑loaner programs are sparse in the peer‑reviewed literature; institutions typically treat this as sensitive operations data. 
- Dedicated computer test centers (CBTCs): Provide wired, managed, uniform workstations and lockable desks; scalable for very large cohorts, but capex, energy, staffing, and real estate are substantial; some institutions reserve CBTCs for high‑stakes or specialized needs while using BYOD for mainstream assessments. <cite id="09e14b96-0">Dedicated exam centres with wired internet and sufficient space eliminate many BYOD limitations but cost remains a major barrier</cite> <cite id="05b2a8df-4">In-person BYOD exams used a 20:1 student-to-proctor ratio in classrooms, while CBTCs used two proctors per room with 40–80 computers and later reviewable camera footage; CBTCs can operate asynchronously over several days</cite>.

Remote proctoring at home vs. on‑campus BYOD
- Security/validity parity: <cite id="05b2a8df-1">In a randomized study, students did not gain a significant advantage in BYOD mode with Zoom proctoring compared to computer‑based exams at a CBTC (effect −0.23, 95% CI [−1.68,1.22], p=0.76; −0.02 SD, p=0.65)</cite>. <cite id="05b2a8df-2">Across two randomized crossover experiments, students scored 2.3% higher on non‑coding questions in un‑proctored online exams vs. Zoom‑proctored BYOD; coding questions showed no significant difference; with randomization on most items, the advantage on identical versions escalated to 5.2%; there was no significant difference between Zoom‑proctored and in‑person proctored exams, recommending proctoring plus question randomization to mitigate cheating</cite>. <cite id="6c95020f-0">AI-enabled proctoring assists in detecting unauthorized device usage or multiple individuals, but raises privacy and technical disruption concerns that require clear policies and training</cite>.
- Logistics and ratios: <cite id="05b2a8df-4">BYOD remote sections used Zoom with about 40 students per proctor; in‑person BYOD used 20:1 ratios; CBTCs used two proctors per room for 40–80 computers and allowed asynchronous scheduling over three days</cite>. These data inform staffing budgets and room planning across modalities.

Security/cheating mitigation on BYOD
- Platform lockdown and environment standardization: <cite id="05b2a8df-3">Lockdown browsers (e.g., Safe Exam Browser) restrict OS navigation, internet, and app launching; platforms can randomize content, limit tools, and provide crash recovery</cite>. <cite id="05b2a8df-2">Question randomization substantially mitigated the advantage observed for unproctored vs. Zoom‑proctored BYOD</cite>.
- Remote invigilation and AI analytics: <cite id="6c95020f-0">Webcam/screen recording with AI detects anomalies like multiple people or prolonged absence; institutions must address privacy and system reliability</cite>. 
- Identity and physical space checks: <cite id="6c95020f-0">Remote invigilation includes verifying candidates’ identities virtually and managing exam‑space setup, with AI assisting to flag potential malpractice</cite>. 
- Hybrid on‑campus controls: <cite id="05b2a8df-4">In‑person BYOD with 20:1 proctor ratios and visible invigilation, plus optional video review from CBTC cameras, provides layered assurance</cite>.

Cost and resource implications
- Capital and running costs: <cite id="09e14b96-0">Dedicated exam centers with wired connectivity and sufficient capacity are capital‑intensive; institutions cite cost as a major barrier, leading to BYOD as an economically viable option when fleet investments would be unsustainable</cite>. <cite id="05b2a8df-4">BYOD remote proctoring required 40 students per proctor; in‑person BYOD 20:1; CBTCs used two proctors per room and video review overheads; staffing profiles differ across modes</cite>.
- Technology and training: <cite id="6c95020f-0">Remote invigilation requires training for digital tools, identity verification, and handling technical disruptions; clear policies on data security and privacy are essential</cite>. 
- Uptake and equity: <cite id="6c95020f-4">Loaner programs by the hour can support students without devices, but cancellations of one‑to‑one programs and shifts to lower‑cost tablets/smartphones affect classroom device availability and require flexible BYOD policies</cite> <cite id="6c95020f-2">Device diversity is extreme; accessibility and security remain core hurdles unless networks and platforms are managed effectively</cite>.

Implementation playbook (evidence‑informed)
- Governance and consent: <cite id="6c95020f-0">Adopt clear policies for data collection, identity verification, and anomaly review in remote invigilation; address privacy concerns through transparent data security practices and training</cite>.
- Secure platform baseline: <cite id="05b2a8df-3">Deploy a lockdown browser/exam environment with restricted OS/network access, question randomization, and crash recovery; integrate identity verification and candidate guidance materials</cite>.
- Logistics blueprint:
  - On‑campus BYOD: reserve supervised rooms with known Wi‑Fi specs; publish step‑by‑step device‑readiness checklists (OS/browser updates, external keyboard, blocked extensions); staff help desks for quick triage; enforce proctor‑to‑student ratios and visible invigilation; use video capture where feasible for audit and training. <cite id="09e14b96-0">Connectivity reliability and venue design are primary levers to reduce BYOD limitations</cite> <cite id="05b2a8df-4">20:1 proctor ratios and on‑site supervision are practical baselines; video review can supplement</cite>.
  - Remote BYOD: schedule synchronous windows; require frontal‑facing/webcam capture, environment checks, and signed proctoring agreements; use AI proctoring to flag anomalies; route flagged cases to manual review; provide technical runbooks for connectivity backup (e.g., mobile hotspot, secondary device). <cite id="05b2a8df-1">BYOD with Zoom proctoring showed no significant performance advantage vs. CBTC</cite> <cite id="05b2a8df-2">Proctoring plus randomization is recommended to mitigate cheating, with small quantifiable advantages for unproctored formats</cite> <cite id="6c95020f-0">AI proctoring supports detection of anomalies while raising privacy/technical considerations</cite>.
  - Loaner/rental bridge: maintain a responsive loaner program with return/repair SLAs; include device sanitization protocols and quick‑start exam image (fully updated OS/browser/VPN/proctoring app) to minimize setup time. <cite id="6c95020f-4">Hourly loan programs can cover equity gaps; prior one‑to‑one program cancellation correlated with reduced classroom laptop use, underscoring the need for flexible access</cite>.
- Validity safeguards: <cite id="05b2a8df-2">Use item randomization, negative marking, time‑boxing, and platform lockdown to equalize conditions across heterogeneous devices; measure and monitor performance parity across BYOD, remote, and CBTC cohorts</cite> <cite id="05b2a8df-1">Randomized evidence indicates no unfair advantage for BYOD under Zoom proctoring relative to CBTC</cite>.

Risks, trade‑offs, and how to manage them
- Connectivity and device variability: <cite id="09e14b96-0">Venue Wi‑Fi bottlenecks and device heterogeneity create variability in load times and app behavior; reserving wired, managed workstations as backup and pre‑validating platforms/ports reduces risk</cite> <cite id="6c95020f-2">Diverse platforms and security restrictions complicate uniform delivery unless the network and exam platform are strictly controlled</cite>.
- Privacy and ethics in remote invigilation: <cite id="6c95020f-0">Continuous monitoring and storage of biometric/video data raise privacy concerns; institutions should adopt minimization principles, explicit consent, and robust data governance; provide candidates with appeal mechanisms and technical support hotlines</cite>.
- Equity and accessibility: <cite id="6c95020f-4">Students may lack personal devices; loaner programs and deposit‑based one‑to‑one models can mitigate this, though changes in program availability affect classroom participation</cite> <cite id="05b2a8df-3">Assistive‑tech parity is improved when the exam environment is standardized via lockdown browsers and accommodations are pre‑approved and supported</cite>.
- Cost and capacity: <cite id="09e14b96-0">Dedicated centers improve exam integrity and comfort but are costly; BYOD reduces capex yet demands careful planning for IT support and proctoring resources</cite> <cite id="05b2a8df-4">Proctoring ratios (20:1 in‑person BYOD; 40:1 remote BYOD) and CBTC staffing levels inform budgeting for human and infrastructural resources</cite>.

When to choose which model
- Prefer BYOD when:
  - Cohort size and throughput demand flexible capacity; <cite id="09e14b96-0">BYOD is often the only economically viable option when dedicated centers are too costly</cite>.
  - You can enforce a secure exam environment and proctoring; <cite id="05b2a8df-2">proctoring plus question randomization mitigates cheating with comparable performance to lab‑based exams</cite> <cite id="05b2a8df-3">lockdown browsers make personal devices secure workstations</cite>.
  - You have a strong support pipeline for connectivity and assistive tech; <cite id="09e14b96-0">connectivity and venue design are critical levers</cite> <cite id="05b2a8df-3">platform crash recovery and restrictions reduce disruption</cite>.
- Prefer rental/loaner + BYOD hybrid when:
  - You need to close the device gap for students without personal tech while keeping the majority BYOD; <cite id="6c95020f-4">hourly loan programs can provide equitable access; prior deposit‑based one‑to‑one programs improved usage but require ongoing management</cite>.
- Prefer dedicated lab/remote proctored at home when:
  - Integrity demands maximum control or the assessment is extremely high‑stakes; <cite id="09e14b96-1">validity and reliability concerns can justify CBTC investment</cite>.
  - Institutions can absorb higher capex and staffing overhead; <cite id="09e14b96-0">cost remains a major barrier to building large CBTCs</cite> <cite id="05b2a8df-4">CBTCs use two proctors per room for 40–80 computers and allow asynchronous delivery</cite>.

Practical checklist for planning a BYOD program at scale
- Governance: <cite id="6c95020f-0">Adopt written remote invigilation policies; train proctors in digital tools and ethics; implement privacy notices and data minimization</cite>.
- Platform: <cite id="05b2a8df-3">Select a secure exam platform with lockdown browsers, identity verification, automatic question randomization, and crash recovery; pre‑test on major OS/browser stacks</cite>.
- Infrastructure: <cite id="09e14b96-0">Stand up exam‑only Wi‑Fi with captive portals and bandwidth reservations; designate wired backup rooms and lockable desks for fallback</cite>.
- Equity: <cite id="6c95020f-4">Launch a loaner program with return/repair SLAs; publish device‑readiness guides and deposit policies</cite>.
- Proctoring: <cite id="05b2a8df-4">Plan proctor staffing by 20:1 (in‑person) or 40:1 (remote) ratios; enable video capture and post‑hoc review</cite> <cite id="05b2a8df-2">use AI proctoring to flag anomalies and combine with human review</cite>.
- Quality assurance: <cite id="09e14b96-3">Run post‑exam surveys with device/os/browser fields; collect open‑ended feedback; iterate on connectivity, instructions, and support</cite> <cite id="05b2a8df-2">monitor performance parity and adjust item randomization/negative marking as needed</cite>.
- Contingency: <cite id="09e14b96-0">Prepare fail‑over to wired exam centers or centralized CBTCs for cohorts where BYOD integrity risk is highest</cite>.

Evidence gaps and research needs
- Rental device program performance: Peer‑reviewed literature provides qualitative guidance on loaner programs and device diversity but lacks large‑scale quantitative reports on failure rates, repair downtimes, and cost per device for university exam access; institutions should collect internal KPIs (utilization, dwell time, rework) and publish learning over cycles. <cite id="6c95020f-4">Evidence highlights loaner programs’ role and prior one‑to‑one program impacts but does not quantify failure rates</cite>.
- Cross‑institutional cost models: While feasibility analyses argue for BYOD on cost grounds, robust, comparable cost models across universities (BYOD vs CBTC vs fully remote) are scarce; multi‑year comparative case studies with unit‑cost accounting and proctoring staff productivity metrics would strengthen decision‑making. <cite id="09e14b96-0">Cost is repeatedly identified as a barrier to building dedicated centers, making BYOD attractive, but detailed cost breakdowns are not standardized</cite>.
- Long‑term integrity and learning outcomes: More longitudinal studies are needed to link BYOD proctoring configurations to cheating incidence and academic outcomes across disciplines (e.g., coding vs. recall‑heavy courses). <cite id="05b2a8df-2">Coding questions showed no significant difference between proctoring modes, suggesting modality effects may vary by task type</cite>.

Bottom line for large, high‑stakes exams
- BYOD is feasible at university scale when paired with a secure, standardized exam environment, robust proctoring (on‑site and/or remote), and strong support and equity measures; large‑class implementations like NUS’s 672‑student BYOD final demonstrate viability with measurable student satisfaction alongside identified operational improvements. <cite id="09e14b96-4">A BYOD open‑book final for 672 students at NUS showed both satisfaction and improvement opportunities</cite> <cite id="05b2a8df-3">Secure platforms and lockdown browsers can make personal devices reliable, controlled workstations</cite>.
- Compared with rental devices and dedicated labs, BYOD offers the best cost‑throughput trade‑off for mainstream cohorts when integrity risks are mitigated by platform controls and proctoring; institutions should reserve centrally managed labs for high‑stakes subsets and use loaner devices to close equity gaps, while adopting clear privacy and support policies for remote invigilation. <cite id="09e14b96-0">Dedicated centers improve conditions but are costly; BYOD can be the economically viable option</cite> <cite id="05b2a8df-2">Proctoring plus randomization yields comparable performance to lab‑based exams and reduces cheating advantages</cite> <cite id="6c95020f-0">Remote invigilation scales geographically but requires strong privacy and technical governance</cite>.
- Start small, pilot with a representative cohort, measure performance parity and candidate satisfaction, and iterate toward a hybrid model; use the empirical survey instrument and operational playbook above to collect comparable data and continuously improve. <cite id="09e14b96-3">Post‑exam surveys with device and infrastructure items at 920 participants (51% response) provide a template for iterative improvement</cite>.

Appendix: Representative success metrics and configurations
- Scale: <cite id="09e14b96-4">672 students BYOD final at NUS with surveys and focus groups</cite>.
- Proctoring parity: <cite id="05b2a8df-1">No significant advantage for BYOD with Zoom vs. CBTC (p=0.76; −0.23 SD)</cite> <cite id="05b2a8df-2">BYOD Zoom proctoring comparable to in‑person; unproctored had higher non‑coding scores (2.3% overall; 5.2% on identical versions), recommending proctoring and randomization</cite>.
- Staffing footprints: <cite id="05b2a8df-4">BYOD in‑person 20:1; remote 40:1; CBTC two proctors per room with 40–80 computers; optional video review</cite>.
- Platform controls: <cite id="05b2a8df-3">Lockdown browsers like Safe Exam Browser restrict access; BlueBook prevents other apps/internet and recovers from crashes; EXaHM disables network and unauthorized tools on lab machines and supported remote exams</cite>.

The programme is the equivalent of an Australian year 12 high school certificate or the International Baccalaureate. The second author is a unit coordinator and teacher of the units in which the e-exam trials were conducted. Title: Transforming Computer-Based Exams with BYOD: An Empirical Study
Snippet: To gain comprehensive insights into the experiences and perspectives of the students regarding the newly introduced BYOD assessment concept, we employed a survey-based approach. All 920 students who participated in the aforementioned final exams were invited via e-mail to take part in the survey. This anonymous survey, which was conducted in March 2023 and hosted on the community version of the open-source survey tool LimeSurvey4 , aimed to collect valuable data pertaining to their experiences and perceptions of the BYOD assessment concept. We sent three reminders to the students who had not yet participated. All survey questions, except for the introductory demographic queries and certain open-ended text responses, employ a 5-point Likert scale [1]. The survey commences with a series of introductory demographic questions, encompassing identification of the specific exam taken among the three options, the student's current study program, ongoing degree pursued, and academic semester. Additionally, respondents are asked to provide information regarding the hardware employed during the exam, including details on the operating system and web browser used.

This section examines their familiarity with computerbased exams, both within the university setting and in remote environments at home. Subsequently, the survey addresses participants' specific experiences with computer-based exams conducted through Artemis. It seeks to gauge their impressions and observations concerning the usage of this platform for assessment. 

The survey proceeds to investigate aspects related to the editing of the exam content and the participants' perceptions of the potential for cheating in the context of computer-based exams. Participants are then queried about their preferred location for taking exams, shedding light on whether they prefer on-campus exam halls or remote settings. The subsequent section pertains to the technical equipment available to participants and the adequacy of infrastructure within the lecture hall during the exam. Following structured questions, the survey includes open-ended queries, inviting participants to articulate their perspectives on both the advantages and disadvantages associated with the implemented exam format. Finally, the survey concludes with a set of questions aimed at capturing participants' overall impressions of the exam experience and their preferences for assessment formats in future educational endeavors. Of the 920 invited participants, 467 completed it (response rate 51%).

Title: Comparing the Security of Three Proctoring Regimens for Bring-Your-Own-Device Exams
Snippet: We compare the exam security of three proctoring regimens of Bring-Your-Own-Device, synchronous, computer-based exams in a computer science class: online un-proctored, online proctored via Zoom, and in-person proctored. We performed two randomized crossover experiments to compare these proctoring regimens. The first study measured the score advantage students receive while taking un-proctored online exams over Zoom-proctored online exams. The second study measured the score advantage of students taking Zoom-proctored online exams over in-person proctored exams. In both studies, students took six 50-minute exams using their own devices, which included two coding questions and 8--10 non-coding questions. We find that students score 2.3% higher on non-coding questions when taking exams in the un-proctored format compared to Zoom proctoring. No statistically significant advantage was found for the coding questions. While most of the non-coding questions had randomization such that students got different versions, for the few questions where all students received the same exact version, the score advantage escalated to 5.2%. From the second study, we find no statistically significant difference between students' performance on Zoom-proctored vs. in-person proctored exams. With this, we recommend educators incorporate some form of proctoring along with question randomization to mitigate cheating concerns in BYOD exams.
</snippet>

The work in this paper builds on this idea by empirically evaluating the effectiveness of BYOD in large-scale assessments, with a focus on pedagogical alignment and student preferences. 

Many learning management systems incorporating an integrated exam mode alongside specialized computer-based exam tools exist [18,21]. The exam software EXaHM is one example of a specialized computer-based exam tool [9]. This software guarantees the absence of network connectivity on laboratory computers during exams and restricts students to utilizing only the tools explicitly authorized by the instructors. Inhibiting the operation of programs such as Windows Explorer and the command window significantly diminishes opportunities for academic dishonesty. EXaHM was employed in the aforementioned evaluation conducted by Hammer et al. (2018) [17], and during the COVID-19 pandemic, its utility was subsequently extended to also facilitate remote exams [20]. Another example of an examination environment is the open-source, crossplatform software BlueBook, a Java-based application running on the student's computer [30]. It prevents students from accessing other applications or the internet during the exam and includes a crash recovery mode in case the application crashes. 

Allowing students to bring their own device for writing an exam poses cheating-related issues [13,33]. There are several approaches to prevent cheating during computer-based exams. Kurniawan et al. [22] introduce the concept of lockdown browsers for BYOD exams. Installing this special-purpose browser on the students' devices turns it into secure workstations with limited system or internet access for the period of the exam. An example instance for such a lockdown browser is the Safe Exam Browser (https://safeexambrowser.org). Another approach makes use of automated video proctoring [27]. The students' screen video recordings are compared for visual similarity of successive frames to detect changes in screen content, which would indicate that the student left the designated exam window.

Title: A Comparative Analysis of Traditional and AI-Based Monitoring in Smart Exam Invigilation Systems
Snippet: Settings. 

The rise of online education has led to a significant transformation in exam invigilation practices, paving the way for remote monitoring solutions [6]. Unlike traditional invigilation, remote invigilation employs digital tools such as webcams, screen recording software, and AI-based analytics to monitor candidates during online examinations [8]. This approach enables institutions to administer exams for geographically dispersed candidates, providing flexibility and scalability [6]. 

Online invigilation introduces several new responsibilities for invigilators, including ensuring proper setup of digital proctoring systems, verifying candidates' identities virtually, and addressing technical issues during exams [10]. AI-enabled systems assist in detecting anomalies such as unauthorized device usage or multiple individuals in a candidate's exam space, flagging potential cases of malpractice for further review [8]. Despite these advancements, remote invigilation faces significant challenges. Candidates often express concerns about data privacy due to continuous monitoring and the storage of sensitive information such as video recordings or biometric data. Moreover, technical disruptions, such as poor internet connectivity or software malfunctions, can compromise the fairness and smooth execution of online exams [6]. 

Research underscores the need for comprehensive invigilator training programs that focus on the use of digital tools and address ethical considerations in remote monitoring [8]. Institutions must also implement clear and transparent policies regarding data security and candidate privacy to build trust in these systems. While online invigilation has enabled institutions to adapt to global education demands, ongoing refinement is essential to balance technological advancements with ethical and operational challenges [6]. 

Remote invigilation is driven by advanced software systems that monitor candidates during exams. These platforms often include features such as webcam recording, screen sharing, and microphone usage to observe the test environment [8]. Artificial intelligence (AI) plays a key role, automating tasks such as facial recognition, behavior analysis, and flagging suspicious activities [9]. 

For example, AI can identify anomalies such as multiple individuals in the room, prolonged absences, or unauthorized device usages. Secure exam platforms also employ measures like browser lockdowns to restrict candidates from accessing external websites, applications, or files during the test.
</snippet>

Title: Automation of Traditional Exam Invigilation using CCTV and Bio-Metric
Snippet: In case of traditional exam based studies, an embedded exam invigilation system was proposed where an improved version of regular traditional exam invigilation was presented. Each student is provided with an electronic ID card as well as an electronic card reader which is serially interfaced with invigilator's computer to authenticate students before entering the exam hall [12]. The system had severe flaws in authentication model as anyone can sit for the exam as long as he holds the electronic ID card. Moreover, the research did not mention about how the exam hall can be monitored and controlled apart from studying authentication part. Similar trend is observed with minor improvement in the following two studies: exam hall invigilation using GSM-GPRS and RFID based exam hall proctoring. In the former one use the location of exam hall for checking authentication as such the whole system would not work if there is a change in the location of exam hall [13]. Later one has some issues as if RFID card stolen or lost then RFID detectors needs to be set up again and this system cannot eliminate impersonation let alone eradicate malpractices during exam [14]. Some researchers suggested an exam hall invigilation system that authenticates examinees based on password [15]. As we all know password can be hacked, tempered or forgotten as such even legitimate examinees are prevented to enter the exam hall and create chaos. As a result the system cannot eliminate impersonation during exam as well. 

The authors has proposed a new automated exam invigilation model using CCTV, fingerprint sensor module, ultra-sensitive microphones and speakers in order to overcome the gaps found in the current and previous literatures in the context of exam invigilation. The proposed model offers simple, secure, efficient and cost effective solution of complex traditional exam invigilation process.
</snippet>

In particular, BYOD technology can significantly contribute to «attracting and retaining talented employees, increasing the productivity and mobility of employees, increasing their satisfaction, as well as reducing IT» [4]. 

In addition, research has shown that the mobile devices that students bring with them to an educational institution are extremely diverse, from traditional laptops to various smartphones and tablets, and even entertainment devices such as game consoles and Internet TVs. These mobile devices are not intended for personal use only. They are increasingly being integrated into the educational process. At the same time, information security continues to be one of the main problems for educational organizations. The study revealed some questionable, already implemented practices of using devices and technologies that undermine security and expose university computer networks to vulnerabilities. For the full-scale implementation of the BYOD strategy, there are many unresolved issues in the management of corporate educational networks.

Title: To take or not to take the laptop or tablet to classes, that is the question
Snippet: The ultimate objective is for the findings to enable the optimized design and application of a BYOD strategy without the university having to bear the high costs of its implementation. The chosen case study is composed of a broad sample of students enrolled in the first cycle of the Business Management undergraduate degree course at the University of Seville (Spain). The study is also justified by the fact that the University of Seville cancelled a One-to-One Laptop program called "One student, One laptop" during the 2011e2012 academic year. Students were each loaned a laptop (to keep until the conclusion of their studies) in return for a deposit of 150 Euros. After the program was cancelled, a significant fall was seen in the number of laptops being used by students in the classroom. 

The present study seeks to respond to questions about the real causes that explain this falling use of laptops from the perspective of an assessment given by the students themselves. The motives could include: the lack of financing for the purchase of a laptop (although free loan programs still exist for borrowing universityowned laptops by the hour); recent advances in technology that have broadened the range of possibilities of m-learning implementation in teaching (Valtonen, Havu-Nuutinen, Dillon, & Vesisenaho, 2011); and using devices such as smartphones (O'Bannon and Bolton, 2014) and tablets (Kearney & Maher, 2013), whose purchase cost is generally lower than that of laptops. The present case study considers two devices for comparison, the laptop and the tablet, as these are the two pieces of electronic equipment most used for academic activities at the current time (Zayim & Ozel, 2015). The smartphone was excluded; as this is a device that the vast majority of students always carry around with them, generally for nonacademic reasons, analyzing any differences between the profiles of students who take smartphones to class and those who do not, would not be likely to contribute any relevant conclusions.

Below is a structured literature review on the feasibility of Bring‑Your‑Own‑Device (BYOD) for large, high‑stakes university exams, drawing on case studies, comparative experiments, and feasibility/policy analyses. We synthesize “success stories” with student counts, outline operational models (BYOD vs rental devices vs dedicated labs/remote proctoring), and weigh integrity, cost, and logistics.

Key takeaways at a glance
- BYOD is feasible at scale for high‑stakes exams when institutions address connectivity, device parity, proctoring, and fairness with a secure exam platform and clear policies; large‑class implementations report both satisfaction and actionable limitations, and dedicated exam centers can be prohibitively expensive, pushing institutions toward BYOD as an economically viable option where throughput and cost are critical constraints. <cite id="09e14b96-0">One common thread that runs through the areas for improvement is related to the exam venue, which ideally could be solved with a dedicated exam centre that is equipped with wired internet connected computers and that is large enough to accommodate a large class; however, the cost of setting-up and running such an exam centre remains a major roadblock, making BYOD e-exams a potentially only feasible and economically-viable option</cite> <cite id="09e14b96-4">A bring-your-own-laptop high-stakes open-book final examination for a General Biology course with an enrolment of 672 students was held at the National University of Singapore, with pre/post surveys and focus groups identifying satisfaction and areas for improvement</cite> <cite id="09e14b96-1">Institutions cannot afford to invest in fleets of computers reserved solely for semi-annual testing, making BYOD critical while bringing challenges of validity and reliability</cite>.

Feasibility conditions and constraints
- Connectivity and device parity: BYOD implementations are sensitive to venue Wi‑Fi reliability, device diversity (Windows/macOS/tablets), and uneven hardware capabilities; these issues can be mitigated by reserving wired‑connected, centrally managed lab workstations for fallback, but upfront capex and running costs can be significant, nudging institutions toward BYOD when capacity and cost dominate. <cite id="09e14b96-0">Exam venue limitations and connectivity quality were recurrent pain points; wired, dedicated exam centers improve limitations but are costly, making BYOD more attractive on cost grounds</cite> <cite id="6c95020f-2">Modern teaching increasingly uses students' personal devices; diversity of software and platforms and information security challenges hinder implementation</cite>.
- Security/integrity: BYOD raises cheating risks unless the exam platform enforces lockdown, restricts OS/app access, and supports identity verification and remote invigilation; evidence shows measurable impact on fairness and detectability of anomalies when these controls are absent or weak. <cite id="05b2a8df-3">Allowing students to bring their own device poses cheating-related issues; lockdown browsers and automated video proctoring are common approaches to create secure workstations and monitor exams</cite> <cite id="6c95020f-0">Remote invigilation uses webcams, screen recording, and AI analytics to detect anomalies such as unauthorized device usage or multiple individuals in a candidate's exam space, but raises privacy and technical disruption concerns</cite>.
- Accessibility and policy: BYOD requires clear EULAs/consent for camera/microphone use, accommodations for disability/accessibility, and processes to support a wide range of assistive technologies; fairness concerns motivate platforms that standardize the candidate environment. <cite id="05b2a8df-3">Security approaches include lockdown browsers and crash-recovery modes; specialized tools restrict unauthorized access and randomize questions to reduce advantage</cite> <cite id="6c95020f-0">AI-enabled systems flag suspicious activities, but institutions must implement clear policies around data security and privacy to maintain trust</cite>.

Success stories and scale
- National University of Singapore (NUS), large class feasibility: <cite id="09e14b96-4">In November 2013, NUS ran a BYOD high‑stakes open‑book final exam for 672 students, collecting pre/post surveys and focus groups; results showed both satisfaction and surfaced areas for improvement (e.g., connectivity, instructions, device readiness), and the paper details implementation and limitations</cite>. 
- Monash College (Australia), pre‑university to university pathway: <cite id="09e14b96-2">Trials of supervised short‑text and essay responses using BYOD in two units of the Foundation Year programme (Monash College) explored authentic e‑assessment in exam rooms, supported by a national Australian government‑funded grant investigating BYOD in university examinations</cite>.
- Empirical feedback at scale: <cite id="09e14b96-3">An institutional study invited all 920 students who took BYOD final exams to complete a survey (51% response); items covered device hardware/software, experience with computer‑based exams, perceptions of cheating, preferred exam location, adequacy of lecture‑hall infrastructure, and advantages/disadvantages, yielding actionable insights for continuous improvement</cite>.
- Australia’s “Transforming Exams” national initiative: <cite id="09e14b96-1">Australia is undergoing a cultural and technical shift for high‑stakes assessment; BYOD is positioned as critical to meet capacity without fleets of dedicated test computers, while acknowledging validity and reliability challenges that projects like Transforming Exams aim to address</cite>.

Comparative modes: BYOD vs. rental devices vs. dedicated labs/remote proctoring
Operational models and throughput
- BYOD: Pros and cons. Pros include zero upfront device capex, high throughput because students already own devices, and flexibility to run hybrid (on‑campus and remote) invigilation; cons include heterogeneity, connectivity variability, and integrity risks unless mitigated with secure platforms and proctoring. <cite id="09e14b96-0">BYOD addresses capacity but venue/connectivity issues persist; dedicated exam halls reduce limitations but are costly</cite> <cite id="05b2a8df-3">Lockdown browsers and secure frameworks can transform personal devices into controlled workstations; platforms like Safe Exam Browser restrict access and support crash recovery</cite>.
- Rental/loaner device programs: Institutions often supplement BYOD with hourly/fee loaner devices for students without personal devices; this balances equity and cost but adds logistics (turnaround, sanitization, technical support). <cite id="6c95020f-4">Universities run loan programs where students borrow university-owned laptops by the hour; deposits and program changes affect uptake, and device diversity and affordability motivate mixed strategies</cite> <cite id="6c95020f-2">Students’ devices are extremely diverse; universities canceled a one‑to‑one laptop program and observed a fall in classroom laptop use, reinforcing the need for flexible access and clear BYOD strategies</cite>. Evidence gaps: published, quantitative failure rates and cost per device for university exam‑loaner programs are sparse in the peer‑reviewed literature; institutions typically treat this as sensitive operations data. 
- Dedicated computer test centers (CBTCs): Provide wired, managed, uniform workstations and lockable desks; scalable for very large cohorts, but capex, energy, staffing, and real estate are substantial; some institutions reserve CBTCs for high‑stakes or specialized needs while using BYOD for mainstream assessments. <cite id="09e14b96-0">Dedicated exam centres with wired internet and sufficient space eliminate many BYOD limitations but cost remains a major barrier</cite> <cite id="05b2a8df-4">In-person BYOD exams used a 20:1 student-to-proctor ratio in classrooms, while CBTCs used two proctors per room with 40–80 computers and later reviewable camera footage; CBTCs can operate asynchronously over several days</cite>.

Remote proctoring at home vs. on‑campus BYOD
- Security/validity parity: <cite id="05b2a8df-1">In a randomized study, students did not gain a significant advantage in BYOD mode with Zoom proctoring compared to computer‑based exams at a CBTC (effect −0.23, 95% CI [−1.68,1.22], p=0.76; −0.02 SD, p=0.65)</cite>. <cite id="05b2a8df-2">Across two randomized crossover experiments, students scored 2.3% higher on non‑coding questions in un‑proctored online exams vs. Zoom‑proctored BYOD; coding questions showed no significant difference; with randomization on most items, the advantage on identical versions escalated to 5.2%; there was no significant difference between Zoom‑proctored and in‑person proctored exams, recommending proctoring plus question randomization to mitigate cheating</cite>. <cite id="6c95020f-0">AI-enabled proctoring assists in detecting unauthorized device usage or multiple individuals, but raises privacy and technical disruption concerns that require clear policies and training</cite>.
- Logistics and ratios: <cite id="05b2a8df-4">BYOD remote sections used Zoom with about 40 students per proctor; in‑person BYOD used 20:1 ratios; CBTCs used two proctors per room for 40–80 computers and allowed asynchronous scheduling over three days</cite>. These data inform staffing budgets and room planning across modalities.

Security/cheating mitigation on BYOD
- Platform lockdown and environment standardization: <cite id="05b2a8df-3">Lockdown browsers (e.g., Safe Exam Browser) restrict OS navigation, internet, and app launching; platforms can randomize content, limit tools, and provide crash recovery</cite>. <cite id="05b2a8df-2">Question randomization substantially mitigated the advantage observed for unproctored vs. Zoom‑proctored BYOD</cite>.
- Remote invigilation and AI analytics: <cite id="6c95020f-0">Webcam/screen recording with AI detects anomalies like multiple people or prolonged absence; institutions must address privacy and system reliability</cite>. 
- Identity and physical space checks: <cite id="6c95020f-0">Remote invigilation includes verifying candidates’ identities virtually and managing exam‑space setup, with AI assisting to flag potential malpractice</cite>. 
- Hybrid on‑campus controls: <cite id="05b2a8df-4">In‑person BYOD with 20:1 proctor ratios and visible invigilation, plus optional video review from CBTC cameras, provides layered assurance</cite>.

Cost and resource implications
- Capital and running costs: <cite id="09e14b96-0">Dedicated exam centers with wired connectivity and sufficient capacity are capital‑intensive; institutions cite cost as a major barrier, leading to BYOD as an economically viable option when fleet investments would be unsustainable</cite>. <cite id="05b2a8df-4">BYOD remote proctoring required 40 students per proctor; in‑person BYOD 20:1; CBTCs used two proctors per room and video review overheads; staffing profiles differ across modes</cite>.
- Technology and training: <cite id="6c95020f-0">Remote invigilation requires training for digital tools, identity verification, and handling technical disruptions; clear policies on data security and privacy are essential</cite>. 
- Uptake and equity: <cite id="6c95020f-4">Loaner programs by the hour can support students without devices, but cancellations of one‑to‑one programs and shifts to lower‑cost tablets/smartphones affect classroom device availability and require flexible BYOD policies</cite> <cite id="6c95020f-2">Device diversity is extreme; accessibility and security remain core hurdles unless networks and platforms are managed effectively</cite>.

Implementation playbook (evidence‑informed)
- Governance and consent: <cite id="6c95020f-0">Adopt clear policies for data collection, identity verification, and anomaly review in remote invigilation; address privacy concerns through transparent data security practices and training</cite>.
- Secure platform baseline: <cite id="05b2a8df-3">Deploy a lockdown browser/exam environment with restricted OS/network access, question randomization, and crash recovery; integrate identity verification and candidate guidance materials</cite>.
- Logistics blueprint:
  - On‑campus BYOD: reserve supervised rooms with known Wi‑Fi specs; publish step‑by‑step device‑readiness checklists (OS/browser updates, external keyboard, blocked extensions); staff help desks for quick triage; enforce proctor‑to‑student ratios and visible invigilation; use video capture where feasible for audit and training. <cite id="09e14b96-0">Connectivity reliability and venue design are primary levers to reduce BYOD limitations</cite> <cite id="05b2a8df-4">20:1 proctor ratios and on‑site supervision are practical baselines; video review can supplement</cite>.
  - Remote BYOD: schedule synchronous windows; require frontal‑facing/webcam capture, environment checks, and signed proctoring agreements; use AI proctoring to flag anomalies; route flagged cases to manual review; provide technical runbooks for connectivity backup (e.g., mobile hotspot, secondary device). <cite id="05b2a8df-1">BYOD with Zoom proctoring showed no significant performance advantage vs. CBTC</cite> <cite id="05b2a8df-2">Proctoring plus randomization is recommended to mitigate cheating, with small quantifiable advantages for unproctored formats</cite> <cite id="6c95020f-0">AI proctoring supports detection of anomalies while raising privacy/technical considerations</cite>.
  - Loaner/rental bridge: maintain a responsive loaner program with return/repair SLAs; include device sanitization protocols and quick‑start exam image (fully updated OS/browser/VPN/proctoring app) to minimize setup time. <cite id="6c95020f-4">Hourly loan programs can cover equity gaps; prior one‑to‑one program cancellation correlated with reduced classroom laptop use, underscoring the need for flexible access</cite>.
- Validity safeguards: <cite id="05b2a8df-2">Use item randomization, negative marking, time‑boxing, and platform lockdown to equalize conditions across heterogeneous devices; measure and monitor performance parity across BYOD, remote, and CBTC cohorts</cite> <cite id="05b2a8df-1">Randomized evidence indicates no unfair advantage for BYOD under Zoom proctoring relative to CBTC</cite>.

Risks, trade‑offs, and how to manage them
- Connectivity and device variability: <cite id="09e14b96-0">Venue Wi‑Fi bottlenecks and device heterogeneity create variability in load times and app behavior; reserving wired, managed workstations as backup and pre‑validating platforms/ports reduces risk</cite> <cite id="6c95020f-2">Diverse platforms and security restrictions complicate uniform delivery unless the network and exam platform are strictly controlled</cite>.
- Privacy and ethics in remote invigilation: <cite id="6c95020f-0">Continuous monitoring and storage of biometric/video data raise privacy concerns; institutions should adopt minimization principles, explicit consent, and robust data governance; provide candidates with appeal mechanisms and technical support hotlines</cite>.
- Equity and accessibility: <cite id="6c95020f-4">Students may lack personal devices; loaner programs and deposit‑based one‑to‑one models can mitigate this, though changes in program availability affect classroom participation</cite> <cite id="05b2a8df-3">Assistive‑tech parity is improved when the exam environment is standardized via lockdown browsers and accommodations are pre‑approved and supported</cite>.
- Cost and capacity: <cite id="09e14b96-0">Dedicated centers improve exam integrity and comfort but are costly; BYOD reduces capex yet demands careful planning for IT support and proctoring resources</cite> <cite id="05b2a8df-4">Proctoring ratios (20:1 in‑person BYOD; 40:1 remote BYOD) and CBTC staffing levels inform budgeting for human and infrastructural resources</cite>.

When to choose which model
- Prefer BYOD when:
  - Cohort size and throughput demand flexible capacity; <cite id="09e14b96-0">BYOD is often the only economically viable option when dedicated centers are too costly</cite>.
  - You can enforce a secure exam environment and proctoring; <cite id="05b2a8df-2">proctoring plus question randomization mitigates cheating with comparable performance to lab‑based exams</cite> <cite id="05b2a8df-3">lockdown browsers make personal devices secure workstations</cite>.
  - You have a strong support pipeline for connectivity and assistive tech; <cite id="09e14b96-0">connectivity and venue design are critical levers</cite> <cite id="05b2a8df-3">platform crash recovery and restrictions reduce disruption</cite>.
- Prefer rental/loaner + BYOD hybrid when:
  - You need to close the device gap for students without personal tech while keeping the majority BYOD; <cite id="6c95020f-4">hourly loan programs can provide equitable access; prior deposit‑based one‑to‑one programs improved usage but require ongoing management</cite>.
- Prefer dedicated lab/remote proctored at home when:
  - Integrity demands maximum control or the assessment is extremely high‑stakes; <cite id="09e14b96-1">validity and reliability concerns can justify CBTC investment</cite>.
  - Institutions can absorb higher capex and staffing overhead; <cite id="09e14b96-0">cost remains a major barrier to building large CBTCs</cite> <cite id="05b2a8df-4">CBTCs use two proctors per room for 40–80 computers and allow asynchronous delivery</cite>.

Practical checklist for planning a BYOD program at scale
- Governance: <cite id="6c95020f-0">Adopt written remote invigilation policies; train proctors in digital tools and ethics; implement privacy notices and data minimization</cite>.
- Platform: <cite id="05b2a8df-3">Select a secure exam platform with lockdown browsers, identity verification, automatic question randomization, and crash recovery; pre‑test on major OS/browser stacks</cite>.
- Infrastructure: <cite id="09e14b96-0">Stand up exam‑only Wi‑Fi with captive portals and bandwidth reservations; designate wired backup rooms and lockable desks for fallback</cite>.
- Equity: <cite id="6c95020f-4">Launch a loaner program with return/repair SLAs; publish device‑readiness guides and deposit policies</cite>.
- Proctoring: <cite id="05b2a8df-4">Plan proctor staffing by 20:1 (in‑person) or 40:1 (remote) ratios; enable video capture and post‑hoc review</cite> <cite id="05b2a8df-2">use AI proctoring to flag anomalies and combine with human review</cite>.
- Quality assurance: <cite id="09e14b96-3">Run post‑exam surveys with device/os/browser fields; collect open‑ended feedback; iterate on connectivity, instructions, and support</cite> <cite id="05b2a8df-2">monitor performance parity and adjust item randomization/negative marking as needed</cite>.
- Contingency: <cite id="09e14b96-0">Prepare fail‑over to wired exam centers or centralized CBTCs for cohorts where BYOD integrity risk is highest</cite>.

Evidence gaps and research needs
- Rental device program performance: Peer‑reviewed literature provides qualitative guidance on loaner programs and device diversity but lacks large‑scale quantitative reports on failure rates, repair downtimes, and cost per device for university exam access; institutions should collect internal KPIs (utilization, dwell time, rework) and publish learning over cycles. <cite id="6c95020f-4">Evidence highlights loaner programs’ role and prior one‑to‑one program impacts but does not quantify failure rates</cite>.
- Cross‑institutional cost models: While feasibility analyses argue for BYOD on cost grounds, robust, comparable cost models across universities (BYOD vs CBTC vs fully remote) are scarce; multi‑year comparative case studies with unit‑cost accounting and proctoring staff productivity metrics would strengthen decision‑making. <cite id="09e14b96-0">Cost is repeatedly identified as a barrier to building dedicated centers, making BYOD attractive, but detailed cost breakdowns are not standardized</cite>.
- Long‑term integrity and learning outcomes: More longitudinal studies are needed to link BYOD proctoring configurations to cheating incidence and academic outcomes across disciplines (e.g., coding vs. recall‑heavy courses). <cite id="05b2a8df-2">Coding questions showed no significant difference between proctoring modes, suggesting modality effects may vary by task type</cite>.

Bottom line for large, high‑stakes exams
- BYOD is feasible at university scale when paired with a secure, standardized exam environment, robust proctoring (on‑site and/or remote), and strong support and equity measures; large‑class implementations like NUS’s 672‑student BYOD final demonstrate viability with measurable student satisfaction alongside identified operational improvements. <cite id="09e14b96-4">A BYOD open‑book final for 672 students at NUS showed both satisfaction and improvement opportunities</cite> <cite id="05b2a8df-3">Secure platforms and lockdown browsers can make personal devices reliable, controlled workstations</cite>.
- Compared with rental devices and dedicated labs, BYOD offers the best cost‑throughput trade‑off for mainstream cohorts when integrity risks are mitigated by platform controls and proctoring; institutions should reserve centrally managed labs for high‑stakes subsets and use loaner devices to close equity gaps, while adopting clear privacy and support policies for remote invigilation. <cite id="09e14b96-0">Dedicated centers improve conditions but are costly; BYOD can be the economically viable option</cite> <cite id="05b2a8df-2">Proctoring plus randomization yields comparable performance to lab‑based exams and reduces cheating advantages</cite> <cite id="6c95020f-0">Remote invigilation scales geographically but requires strong privacy and technical governance</cite>.
- Start small, pilot with a representative cohort, measure performance parity and candidate satisfaction, and iterate toward a hybrid model; use the empirical survey instrument and operational playbook above to collect comparable data and continuously improve. <cite id="09e14b96-3">Post‑exam surveys with device and infrastructure items at 920 participants (51% response) provide a template for iterative improvement</cite>.

Appendix: Representative success metrics and configurations
- Scale: <cite id="09e14b96-4">672 students BYOD final at NUS with surveys and focus groups</cite>.
- Proctoring parity: <cite id="05b2a8df-1">No significant advantage for BYOD with Zoom vs. CBTC (p=0.76; −0.23 SD)</cite> <cite id="05b2a8df-2">BYOD Zoom proctoring comparable to in‑person; unproctored had higher non‑coding scores (2.3% overall; 5.2% on identical versions), recommending proctoring and randomization</cite>.
- Staffing footprints: <cite id="05b2a8df-4">BYOD in‑person 20:1; remote 40:1; CBTC two proctors per room with 40–80 computers; optional video review</cite>.
- Platform controls: <cite id="05b2a8df-3">Lockdown browsers like Safe Exam Browser restrict access; BlueBook prevents other apps/internet and recovers from crashes; EXaHM disables network and unauthorized tools on lab machines and supported remote exams</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Students’ perceptions of BYOD open-book examinations in a large class
Snippet: Considering the increasing prevalence of tablets, one of the possible next steps should include the use of tablets as one of the devices in a BYOD e-exam. Currently, the use of tablets is still not possible due to security issues, especially in a high-stakes exam. However, it is understood that there are e-exam software companies who are developing the necessary apps for a BYOD e-exam on tablets. 

One common thread that runs through the areas for improvement is related to the exam venue, which ideally could be solved with a dedicated exam centre that is equipped with wired internet connected computers and that is large enough to accommodate a large class. With that, many of the limitations of a BYOD exam discussed in this paper will be eliminated, and the whole subject of a BYOD exam will not even surface. While the university is not discounting this option, the cost of setting-up and running such an exam centre remains as a major roadblock. Going forward, a BYOD e-exam, and all its associated limitations may be the only feasible and economically-viable option.

Title: A pedagogical end game for exams
Snippet: Australia stands on a cusp for high stakes assessment. Institutions cannot afford to invest in fleets of computers reserved solely for semi-annual testing. Bring your own device (BYOD) solutions are therefore critical to this cultural transformation, bringing challenges of validity and reliability. But the prize is worth striving for, making academic awards more credible, and carrying the opportunity to reform curricula with powerful software tools. Further information on the national 'Transforming Exams' (2015) project is available.

Title: Writing e-Exams in Pre-University College
Snippet: In Australia, the first author is leading an Australian federal government funded grant project [1] investigating how authentic e-assessment can be introduced into the examination rooms of universities using bring-your-own-devices (BYOD). This study was undertaken within two units offered in the Foundation Year [20] programme at Monash College, Australia. The programme is the equivalent of an Australian year 12 high school certificate or the International Baccalaureate. The second author is a unit coordinator and teacher of the units in which the e-exam trials were conducted. The trials were carried out using in-class supervised written assessments requiring short text and essay-style responses.

Title: Transforming Computer-Based Exams with BYOD: An Empirical Study
Snippet: To gain comprehensive insights into the experiences and perspectives of the students regarding the newly introduced BYOD assessment concept, we employed a survey-based approach. All 920 students who participated in the aforementioned final exams were invited via e-mail to take part in the survey. This anonymous survey, which was conducted in March 2023 and hosted on the community version of the open-source survey tool LimeSurvey4 , aimed to collect valuable data pertaining to their experiences and perceptions of the BYOD assessment concept. We sent three reminders to the students who had not yet participated. All survey questions, except for the introductory demographic queries and certain open-ended text responses, employ a 5-point Likert scale [1]. The survey commences with a series of introductory demographic questions, encompassing identification of the specific exam taken among the three options, the student's current study program, ongoing degree pursued, and academic semester. Additionally, respondents are asked to provide information regarding the hardware employed during the exam, including details on the operating system and web browser used. 

Following the demographic section, the survey includes questions related to the participants' experience with computer-based exams. This section examines their familiarity with computerbased exams, both within the university setting and in remote environments at home. Subsequently, the survey addresses participants' specific experiences with computer-based exams conducted through Artemis. It seeks to gauge their impressions and observations concerning the usage of this platform for assessment. 

The survey proceeds to investigate aspects related to the editing of the exam content and the participants' perceptions of the potential for cheating in the context of computer-based exams. Participants are then queried about their preferred location for taking exams, shedding light on whether they prefer on-campus exam halls or remote settings. The subsequent section pertains to the technical equipment available to participants and the adequacy of infrastructure within the lecture hall during the exam. Following structured questions, the survey includes open-ended queries, inviting participants to articulate their perspectives on both the advantages and disadvantages associated with the implemented exam format. Finally, the survey concludes with a set of questions aimed at capturing participants' overall impressions of the exam experience and their preferences for assessment formats in future educational endeavors. Of the 920 invited participants, 467 completed it (response rate 51%).

Title: Students’ perceptions of BYOD open-book examinations in a large class
Snippet: A bring-your-own-laptop high-stakes open-book final examination for a General Biology course with an enrolment of 672 students was held in November 2013 at the National University of Singapore. Pre- and post-exam online surveys were conducted to solicit the perceptions of the students with regards to the introduction of a bring-your-own-device open-book electronic final examination. Focus group discussions were also held to deliberate on the perceptions in greater detail. Both the surveys and discussions revealed several key areas of satisfaction and also areas for improvement, which will be explicated in this paper. The implementation and limitations of the exam will also be discussed.

Snippet: Using data from Study 1, the regression model in Eq.1 shows that students do not get any significant advantage when taking exams in BYOD mode with Zoom proctoring, compared to exams at CBTC ( = −0.23,95% CI [−1.68,1.22], = 0.76).Using standardized z-scores in a similar analysis, the advantage is found to be −0.02standard deviations and not significant ( = 0.65).We find similar results when comparing BYOD with in-person proctoring and CBTC exams, with  = 0.044, 95% CI [−1.69, 1.78],  = 0.96, and effect size equal to −0.0099 ( = 0.87).

Title: Comparing the Security of Three Proctoring Regimens for Bring-Your-Own-Device Exams
Snippet: We compare the exam security of three proctoring regimens of Bring-Your-Own-Device, synchronous, computer-based exams in a computer science class: online un-proctored, online proctored via Zoom, and in-person proctored. We performed two randomized crossover experiments to compare these proctoring regimens. The first study measured the score advantage students receive while taking un-proctored online exams over Zoom-proctored online exams. The second study measured the score advantage of students taking Zoom-proctored online exams over in-person proctored exams. In both studies, students took six 50-minute exams using their own devices, which included two coding questions and 8--10 non-coding questions. We find that students score 2.3% higher on non-coding questions when taking exams in the un-proctored format compared to Zoom proctoring. No statistically significant advantage was found for the coding questions. While most of the non-coding questions had randomization such that students got different versions, for the few questions where all students received the same exact version, the score advantage escalated to 5.2%. From the second study, we find no statistically significant difference between students' performance on Zoom-proctored vs. in-person proctored exams. With this, we recommend educators incorporate some form of proctoring along with question randomization to mitigate cheating concerns in BYOD exams.

Title: Transforming Computer-Based Exams with BYOD: An Empirical Study
Snippet: His study attributes this gap to concerns over fairness, reliability, and costs. It suggests BYOD as a solution, particularly for financial constraints, and aims to develop a secure and reliable framework for electronic exams on students' devices. The work in this paper builds on this idea by empirically evaluating the effectiveness of BYOD in large-scale assessments, with a focus on pedagogical alignment and student preferences. 

Many learning management systems incorporating an integrated exam mode alongside specialized computer-based exam tools exist [18,21]. The exam software EXaHM is one example of a specialized computer-based exam tool [9]. This software guarantees the absence of network connectivity on laboratory computers during exams and restricts students to utilizing only the tools explicitly authorized by the instructors. Inhibiting the operation of programs such as Windows Explorer and the command window significantly diminishes opportunities for academic dishonesty. EXaHM was employed in the aforementioned evaluation conducted by Hammer et al. (2018) [17], and during the COVID-19 pandemic, its utility was subsequently extended to also facilitate remote exams [20]. Another example of an examination environment is the open-source, crossplatform software BlueBook, a Java-based application running on the student's computer [30]. It prevents students from accessing other applications or the internet during the exam and includes a crash recovery mode in case the application crashes. 

Allowing students to bring their own device for writing an exam poses cheating-related issues [13,33]. There are several approaches to prevent cheating during computer-based exams. Kurniawan et al. [22] introduce the concept of lockdown browsers for BYOD exams. Installing this special-purpose browser on the students' devices turns it into secure workstations with limited system or internet access for the period of the exam. An example instance for such a lockdown browser is the Safe Exam Browser (https://safeexambrowser.org). Another approach makes use of automated video proctoring [27]. The students' screen video recordings are compared for visual similarity of successive frames to detect changes in screen content, which would indicate that the student left the designated exam window.

snippet.text: We compare the exam security of three proctoring regimens of Bring-Your-Own-Device, synchronous, computer-based exams in a computer science class: online un-proctored, online proctored via Zoom, and in-person proctored. We performed two randomized crossover experiments to compare these proctoring regimens. The first study measured the score advantage students receive while taking un-proctored online exams over Zoom-proctored online exams. The second study measured the score advantage of students taking Zoom-proctored online exams over in-person proctored exams. In both studies, students took six 50-minute exams using their own devices, which included two coding questions and 8--10 non-coding questions. We find that students score 2.3% higher on non-coding questions when taking exams in the un-proctored format compared to Zoom proctoring. No statistically significant advantage was found for the coding questions. While most of the non-coding questions had randomization such that students got different versions, for the few questions where all students received the same exact version, the score advantage escalated to 5.2%. From the second study, we find no statistically significant difference between students' performance on Zoom-proctored vs. in-person proctored exams. With this, we recommend educators incorporate some form of proctoring along with question randomization to mitigate cheating concerns in BYOD exams.

His study attributes this gap to concerns over fairness, reliability, and costs. It suggests BYOD as a solution, particularly for financial constraints, and aims to develop a secure and reliable framework for electronic exams on students' devices. The work in this paper builds on this idea by empirically evaluating the effectiveness of BYOD in large-scale assessments, with a focus on pedagogical alignment and student preferences. 

Many learning management systems incorporating an integrated exam mode alongside specialized computer-based exam tools exist [18,21]. The exam software EXaHM is one example of a specialized computer-based exam tool [9]. This software guarantees the absence of network connectivity on laboratory computers during exams and restricts students to utilizing only the tools explicitly authorized by the instructors. Inhibiting the operation of programs such as Windows Explorer and the command window significantly diminishes opportunities for academic dishonesty. EXaHM was employed in the aforementioned evaluation conducted by Hammer et al. (2018) [17], and during the COVID-19 pandemic, its utility was subsequently extended to also facilitate remote exams [20]. Another example of an examination environment is the open-source, crossplatform software BlueBook, a Java-based application running on the student's computer [30]. It prevents students from accessing other applications or the internet during the exam and includes a crash recovery mode in case the application crashes. 

Allowing students to bring their own device for writing an exam poses cheating-related issues [13,33]. There are several approaches to prevent cheating during computer-based exams. Kurniawan et al. [22] introduce the concept of lockdown browsers for BYOD exams. Installing this special-purpose browser on the students' devices turns it into secure workstations with limited system or internet access for the period of the exam. An example instance for such a lockdown browser is the Safe Exam Browser (https://safeexambrowser.org). Another approach makes use of automated video proctoring [27]. The students' screen video recordings are compared for visual similarity of successive frames to detect changes in screen content, which would indicate that the student left the designated exam window.

Title: A Comparative Analysis of Traditional and AI-Based Monitoring in Smart Exam Invigilation Systems
Snippet: Settings. 

The rise of online education has led to a significant transformation in exam invigilation practices, paving the way for remote monitoring solutions [6]. Unlike traditional invigilation, remote invigilation employs digital tools such as webcams, screen recording software, and AI-based analytics to monitor candidates during online examinations [8]. This approach enables institutions to administer exams for geographically dispersed candidates, providing flexibility and scalability [6]. 

Online invigilation introduces several new responsibilities for invigilators, including ensuring proper setup of digital proctoring systems, verifying candidates' identities virtually, and addressing technical issues during exams [10]. AI-enabled systems assist in detecting anomalies such as unauthorized device usage or multiple individuals in a candidate's exam space, flagging potential cases of malpractice for further review [8]. Despite these advancements, remote invigilation faces significant challenges. Candidates often express concerns about data privacy due to continuous monitoring and the storage of sensitive information such as video recordings or biometric data. Moreover, technical disruptions, such as poor internet connectivity or software malfunctions, can compromise the fairness and smooth execution of online exams [6]. 

Research underscores the need for comprehensive invigilator training programs that focus on the use of digital tools and address ethical considerations in remote monitoring [8]. Institutions must also implement clear and transparent policies regarding data security and candidate privacy to build trust in these systems. While online invigilation has enabled institutions to adapt to global education demands, ongoing refinement is essential to balance technological advancements with ethical and operational challenges [6]. 

Remote invigilation is driven by advanced software systems that monitor candidates during exams. These platforms often include features such as webcam recording, screen sharing, and microphone usage to observe the test environment [8]. Artificial intelligence (AI) plays a key role, automating tasks such as facial recognition, behavior analysis, and flagging suspicious activities [9]. 

For example, AI can identify anomalies such as multiple individuals in the room, prolonged absences, or unauthorized device usages. Secure exam platforms also employ measures like browser lockdowns to restrict candidates from accessing external websites, applications, or files during the test.

Title: Automation of Traditional Exam Invigilation using CCTV and Bio-Metric
Snippet: In case of traditional exam based studies, an embedded exam invigilation system was proposed where an improved version of regular traditional exam invigilation was presented. Each student is provided with an electronic ID card as well as an electronic card reader which is serially interfaced with invigilator's computer to authenticate students before entering the exam hall [12]. The system had severe flaws in authentication model as anyone can sit for the exam as long as he holds the electronic ID card. Moreover, the research did not mention about how the exam hall can be monitored and controlled apart from studying authentication part. Similar trend is observed with minor improvement in the following two studies: exam hall invigilation using GSM-GPRS and RFID based exam hall proctoring. In the former one use the location of exam hall for checking authentication as such the whole system would not work if there is a change in the location of exam hall [13]. Later one has some issues as if RFID card stolen or lost then RFID detectors needs to be set up again and this system cannot eliminate impersonation let alone eradicate malpractices during exam [14]. Some researchers suggested an exam hall invigilation system that authenticates examinees based on password [15]. As we all know password can be hacked, tempered or forgotten as such even legitimate examinees are prevented to enter the exam hall and create chaos. As a result the system cannot eliminate impersonation during exam as well. 

The authors has proposed a new automated exam invigilation model using CCTV, fingerprint sensor module, ultra-sensitive microphones and speakers in order to overcome the gaps found in the current and previous literatures in the context of exam invigilation. The proposed model offers simple, secure, efficient and cost effective solution of complex traditional exam invigilation process.

According to a study by California State University (USA), students use their own mobile devices in the learning process on average every six minutes.
