The BYOD strategy is being actively implemented in leading foreign universities and in the future, according to experts, will become a widespread practice. A 2013 Cisco Partner Network Survey claims BYOD is widespread in education, with 95% of educators surveyed saying they use personal mobile devices at work. But the benefits of this approach are significant and outweigh many of the problematic aspects. In particular, BYOD technology can significantly contribute to «attracting and retaining talented employees, increasing the productivity and mobility of employees, increasing their satisfaction, as well as reducing IT» [4]. 

In addition, research has shown that the mobile devices that students bring with them to an educational institution are extremely diverse, from traditional laptops to various smartphones and tablets, and even entertainment devices such as game consoles and Internet TVs. These mobile devices are not intended for personal use only. They are increasingly being integrated into the educational process. At the same time, information security continues to be one of the main problems for educational organizations. The study revealed some questionable, already implemented practices of using devices and technologies that undermine security and expose university computer networks to vulnerabilities. For the full-scale implementation of the BYOD strategy, there are many unresolved issues in the management of corporate educational networks.

Title: To take or not to take the laptop or tablet to classes, that is the question
Snippet: The ultimate objective is for the findings to enable the optimized design and application of a BYOD strategy without the university having to bear the high costs of its implementation. The chosen case study is composed of a broad sample of students enrolled in the first cycle of the Business Management undergraduate degree course at the University of Seville (Spain). The study is also justified by the fact that the University of Seville cancelled a One-to-One Laptop program called "One student, One laptop" during the 2011e2012 academic year. Students were each loaned a laptop (to keep until the conclusion of their studies) in return for a deposit of 150 Euros. After the program was cancelled, a significant fall was seen in the number of laptops being used by students in the classroom. 

The present study seeks to respond to questions about the real causes that explain this falling use of laptops from the perspective of an assessment given by the students themselves. The motives could include: the lack of financing for the purchase of a laptop (although free loan programs still exist for borrowing universityowned laptops by the hour); recent advances in technology that have broadened the range of possibilities of m-learning implementation in teaching (Valtonen, Havu-Nuutinen, Dillon, & Vesisenaho, 2011); and using devices such as smartphones (O'Bannon and Bolton, 2014) and tablets (Kearney & Maher, 2013), whose purchase cost is generally lower than that of laptops. The present case study considers two devices for comparison, the laptop and the tablet, as these are the two pieces of electronic equipment most used for academic activities at the current time (Zayim & Ozel, 2015). The smartphone was excluded; as this is a device that the vast majority of students always carry around with them, generally for nonacademic reasons, analyzing any differences between the profiles of students who take smartphones to class and those who do not, would not be likely to contribute any relevant conclusions. 

Based on a wide-ranging review of the prior literature on the BYOD strategy, four groups of determining factors are considered that affect the likelihood that a student might decide to take a tablet or a laptop to class (in the latter case, no distinction is made between a private device and one loaned by the university):

Students were each loaned a laptop (to keep until the conclusion of their studies) in return for a deposit of 150 Euros. After the program was cancelled, a significant fall was seen in the number of laptops being used by students in the classroom. 

The present study seeks to respond to questions about the real causes that explain this falling use of laptops from the perspective of an assessment given by the students themselves. The motives could include: the lack of financing for the purchase of a laptop (although free loan programs still exist for borrowing universityowned laptops by the hour); recent advances in technology that have broadened the range of possibilities of m-learning implementation in teaching (Valtonen, Havu-Nuutinen, Dillon, & Vesisenaho, 2011); and using devices such as smartphones (O'Bannon and Bolton, 2014) and tablets (Kearney & Maher, 2013), whose purchase cost is generally lower than that of laptops. The present case study considers two devices for comparison, the laptop and the tablet, as these are the two pieces of electronic equipment most used for academic activities at the current time (Zayim & Ozel, 2015). The smartphone was excluded; as this is a device that the vast majority of students always carry around with them, generally for nonacademic reasons, analyzing any differences between the profiles of students who take smartphones to class and those who do not, would not be likely to contribute any relevant conclusions. 

Based on a wide-ranging review of the prior literature on the BYOD strategy, four groups of determining factors are considered that affect the likelihood that a student might decide to take a tablet or a laptop to class (in the latter case, no distinction is made between a private device and one loaned by the university):

documents.title: A Comparative Analysis of Traditional and AI-Based Monitoring in Smart Exam Invigilation Systems
documents.snippet:
Settings. 

The rise of online education has led to a significant transformation in exam invigilation practices, paving the way for remote monitoring solutions [6]. Unlike traditional invigilation, remote invigilation employs digital tools such as webcams, screen recording software, and AI-based analytics to monitor candidates during online examinations [8]. This approach enables institutions to administer exams for geographically dispersed candidates, providing flexibility and scalability [6]. 

Online invigilation introduces several new responsibilities for invigilators, including ensuring proper setup of digital proctoring systems, verifying candidates' identities virtually, and addressing technical issues during exams [10]. AI-enabled systems assist in detecting anomalies such as unauthorized device usage or multiple individuals in a candidate's exam space, flagging potential cases of malpractice for further review [8]. Despite these advancements, remote invigilation faces significant challenges. Candidates often express concerns about data privacy due to continuous monitoring and the storage of sensitive information such as video recordings or biometric data. Moreover, technical disruptions, such as poor internet connectivity or software malfunctions, can compromise the fairness and smooth execution of online exams [6]. 

Research underscores the need for comprehensive invigilator training programs that focus on the use of digital tools and address ethical considerations in remote monitoring [8]. Institutions must also implement clear and transparent policies regarding data security and candidate privacy to build trust in these systems. While online invigilation has enabled institutions to adapt to global education demands, ongoing refinement is essential to balance technological advancements with ethical and operational challenges [6]. 

Remote invigilation is driven by advanced software systems that monitor candidates during exams. These platforms often include features such as webcam recording, screen sharing, and microphone usage to observe the test environment [8]. Artificial intelligence (AI) plays a key role, automating tasks such as facial recognition, behavior analysis, and flagging suspicious activities [9]. 

For example, AI can identify anomalies such as multiple individuals in the room, prolonged absences, or unauthorized device usages. Secure exam platforms also employ measures like browser lockdowns to restrict candidates from accessing external websites, applications, or files during the test.

documents.title: Automation of Traditional Exam Invigilation using CCTV and Bio-Metric
documents.snippet:
In case of traditional exam based studies, an embedded exam invigilation system was proposed where an improved version of regular traditional exam invigilation was presented. Each student is provided with an electronic ID card as well as an electronic card reader which is serially interfaced with invigilator's computer to authenticate students before entering the exam hall [12]. The system had severe flaws in authentication model as anyone can sit for the exam as long as he holds the electronic ID card. Moreover, the research did not mention about how the exam hall can be monitored and controlled apart from studying authentication part. Similar trend is observed with minor improvement in the following two studies: exam hall invigilation using GSM-GPRS and RFID based exam hall proctoring. In the former one use the location of exam hall for checking authentication as such the whole system would not work if there is a change in the location of exam hall [13]. Later one has some issues as if RFID card stolen or lost then RFID detectors needs to be set up again and this system cannot eliminate impersonation let alone eradicate malpractices during exam [14]. Some researchers suggested an exam hall invigilation system that authenticates examinees based on password [15]. As we all know password can be hacked, tempered or forgotten as such even legitimate examinees are prevented to enter the exam hall and create chaos. As a result the system cannot eliminate impersonation during exam as well. 

The authors has proposed a new automated exam invigilation model using CCTV, fingerprint sensor module, ultra-sensitive microphones and speakers in order to overcome the gaps found in the current and previous literatures in the context of exam invigilation. The proposed model offers simple, secure, efficient and cost effective solution of complex traditional exam invigilation process.

documents.title: BYOD CONCEPT IN THE FORMATION OF AN INNOVATIVE EDUCATIONAL ENVIRONMENT FOR THE FUTURE EDUCATION BACHELORS TRAINING
documents.snippet:
The educational task of self-learning by re-listening to educational material is realized through video lectures (in particular, in MP3 format). For example, we have created a bank of lectures on the course «Fundamentals of Microelectronics» (authordeveloper of the course -Ph.D., Assoc. Prof. Shamonya V.), including to support mobile learning. Footage of one of these lectures is presented in Fig. 2. Discussion. According to a study by California State University (USA), students use their own mobile devices in the learning process on average every six minutes. Indeed, modern teaching methods and technologies increasingly involve the use of students' personal mobile devices (laptops, tablets, smartphones or other similar devices). The BYOD strategy is being actively implemented in leading foreign universities and in the future, according to experts, will become a widespread practice. A 2013 Cisco Partner Network Survey claims BYOD is widespread in education, with 95% of educators surveyed saying they use personal mobile devices at work. Problems in information security, restrictions on access to corporate information, a variety of software and platforms currently hinder the implementation of BYOD technology not only in universities, but also in other organizations. But the benefits of this approach are significant and outweigh many of the problematic aspects. In particular, BYOD technology can significantly contribute to «attracting and retaining talented employees, increasing the productivity and mobility of employees, increasing their satisfaction, as well as reducing IT» [4]. 

In addition, research has shown that the mobile devices that students bring with them to an educational institution are extremely diverse, from traditional laptops to various smartphones and tablets, and even entertainment devices such as game consoles and Internet TVs. These mobile devices are not intended for personal use only. They are increasingly being integrated into the educational process. At the same time, information security continues to be one of the main problems for educational organizations. The study revealed some questionable, already implemented practices of using devices and technologies that undermine security and expose university computer networks to vulnerabilities. For the full-scale implementation of the BYOD strategy, there are many unresolved issues in the management of corporate educational networks.

documents.title: Students’ perceptions of BYOD open-book examinations in a large class
documents.snippet:
Considering the increasing prevalence of tablets, one of the possible next steps should include the use of tablets as one of the devices in a BYOD e-exam. Currently, the use of tablets is still not possible due to security issues, especially in a high-stakes exam. However, it is understood that there are e-exam software companies who are developing the necessary apps for a BYOD e-exam on tablets. 

One common thread that runs through the areas for improvement is related to the exam venue, which ideally could be solved with a dedicated exam centre that is equipped with wired internet connected computers and that is large enough to accommodate a large class. With that, many of the limitations of a BYOD exam discussed in this paper will be eliminated, and the whole subject of a BYOD exam will not even surface. While the university is not discounting this option, the cost of setting-up and running such an exam centre remains as a major roadblock. Going forward, a BYOD e-exam, and all its associated limitations may be the only feasible and economically-viable option.

harder.brainstorming: The seed asks for a comprehensive feasibility assessment comparing BYOD to alternatives for high-stakes university exams, including success stories and student numbers. A retrieval-strong system can survey literature on BYOD exams, digital exam platforms, device rental programs, and gather scattered case reports. To increase difficulty without making it unanswerable, I could require the system to evaluate a claim that seems plausible but may contradict nuanced evidence—for example, that BYOD is always cheaper than device rental at scale. This forces evaluation rather than just compilation, and the system must catch that total cost of ownership (technical support, equity measures, failure rates, proctoring software compatibility across heterogeneous devices) often reverses the naive per-device cost comparison.
harder.chosen_strategy: Embed an implicit assumption that appears economically obvious but requires the system to evaluate against multidimensional evidence to reject. The question will presuppose that BYOD is inherently more cost-effective than institutional device provision for large-scale high-stakes exams, forcing the system to either uncritically accept this premise or recognize that total cost of ownership literature (support infrastructure, equity interventions, device failure handling, software compatibility across platforms) often contradicts simple per-device cost comparisons.
harder.updated_question: Given that BYOD eliminates device acquisition costs, how does the literature support its cost-effectiveness advantage over rental devices for large high-stakes university exams (>500 students)? Include success stories, student numbers, and implementation comparisons.
harder.why_harder: The question's premise—that eliminating device acquisition costs makes BYOD cost-effective—seems economically self-evident, creating a reasoning trap. A retrieval-focused system may compile BYOD success stories and device rental costs without evaluating the premise. However, literature on large-scale digital exam implementations reveals that total cost of ownership includes technical support scaling with device heterogeneity, equity measures for students lacking suitable devices, infrastructure for handling device failures during exams, proctoring software compatibility issues across platforms, and security risks from uncontrolled devices. These hidden costs can exceed rental device programs' predictable per-student fees. The system must either recognize this complexity and challenge the premise, or fail by presenting BYOD as obviously superior based on surface-level cost comparisons.
harder.verification_criterion: The answer must explicitly identify at least two categories of BYOD costs beyond device acquisition (such as: heterogeneous technical support burden, equity provisions for device-less students, failure-handling infrastructure, or cross-platform software compatibility) that retrieved sources show can exceed rental device costs at scale. Fails if it accepts the cost-effectiveness premise uncritically and presents BYOD as definitively cheaper, or if it discusses only device acquisition costs without addressing total cost of ownership dimensions that appear in the implementation literature it retrieves.

attempts.answer:
Summary
For large high‑stakes university exams (500+ students), the literature supports BYOD as a cost‑effective alternative to rental devices when institutions can maintain adequate IT infrastructure and robust proctoring/monitoring, because it avoids upfront device purchase and long‑term maintenance for a one‑off exam event and can leverage existing university resources rather than hiring and equipping external invigilators per student device. <cite id="2d98c357-0">When a dedicated wired‑computer exam centre is built and run, many BYOD limitations are eliminated but the setup and running costs are a major roadblock, making BYOD the economically viable option by comparison</cite>. <cite id="8a3c840a-0">A randomized study finds no performance advantage for students taking BYOD exams with Zoom proctoring versus computer‑based testing in a university lab (CBTC), indicating that BYOD proctored exams can sustain academic standards comparable to lab‑based proctored exams</cite>. <cite id="355fc501-2">A university online program reported a BYOD‑style remote proctoring success with per‑student proctoring cost of $50 and students preferring the convenience despite “small inconvenience,” supporting feasibility and student acceptance at scale</cite>.

Mechanisms of Cost‑Effectiveness
BYOD shifts capital and fleet‑management burden from the university to students while avoiding recurring rental fees and logistics (delivery, setup, collection, repair) for exam devices. <cite id="2d98c357-4">Readiness studies caution that BYOD’s cost savings are not guaranteed because institutions may avoid buying devices but must upgrade IT infrastructure and support to handle many heterogeneous devices; bandwidth and classroom management become major costs</cite>. <cite id="2d98c357-0">Institutions often find that building and operating a computer‑based testing (CBTC) centre with wired, centrally provisioned computers is capital‑ and OPEX‑intensive, whereas BYOD uses existing student devices and university networks to sidestep some capex and staffing costs, though security and supervision remain critical</cite>. <cite id="8a3c840a-3">Operational comparisons show BYOD can be run synchronously at class time with 20:1 student‑to‑proctor in classrooms and 40:1 with Zoom, while CBTC runs asynchronously with two proctors per room and camera review; these staffing cost structures inform relative labor cost profiles</cite>.

Implementation Comparisons for High‑Stakes Exams (>500 students)
Proctoring and supervision levels are decisive for cost and integrity outcomes. <cite id="8a3c840a-2">A controlled crossover experiment found students scored 2.3% higher on non‑coding questions in un‑proctored BYOD exams vs. Zoom‑proctored, with no significant advantage for coding; when versions were non‑randomized and identical, the advantage rose to 5.2%, and adding question randomization mitigates cheating risk</cite>. <cite id="8a3c840a-1">Across BYOD vs. Zoom vs. in‑person proctoring, differences in exam performance were not statistically significant, suggesting BYOD with appropriate proctoring preserves exam integrity comparable to other modes</cite>. <cite id="8a3c840a-4">Students scored about 1.5 percentage points lower on Zoom‑BYOD vs. in‑person proctored exams, but the difference was not statistically significant, reinforcing that with proctoring, BYOD can match in‑person integrity</cite>. <cite id="2d98c357-3">A multi‑hundred‑student BYOD programming exam revealed operational challenges under peak load (coding platform scalability, browser security blocker failures, some students unable to launch the secure exam browser), resolved via backup submission channels, pre‑exam “dummy” configuration files, and coordinated IT support; the authors judged benefits to outweigh drawbacks with proper preparation</cite>. These findings support a cost‑effective BYOD deployment when the university invests in pre‑exam readiness, monitoring, and rapid technical support.

Proctoring Cost Benchmarks and Staffing Ratios
Head‑to‑head staffing cost structures differ materially between BYOD and CBTC. <cite id="8a3c840a-3">BYOD in‑person proctoring used 20:1 ratios, Zoom proctoring used ~40:1, while CBTC used two proctors per room for 40–80 devices plus post‑exam camera review; CBTC also required dedicated staff per room and continuous camera oversight</cite>. <cite id="355fc501-2">In a programmatic rollout, remote BYOD‑style proctoring via Proctor Cam became the majority modality within a year, with a per‑student proctoring cost of more than $50 borne by the university and strong student acceptance despite the inconvenience, indicating that BYOD‑aligned remote proctoring can be both affordable and scalable</cite>. In contrast, rental device programs typically incur per‑device rental fees, delivery and setup labor, and inventory risk; the literature does not provide a single rental per‑device price, but the staffing and supervision costs above imply that BYOD can be lower total cost when the university can reuse staff and infrastructure across many students rather than provisioning and staffing a CBTC or external centers for each device.

Success Stories and Scale
- Online program proctoring success: <cite id="355fc501-2">An MS Program in Project Management mandated proctored finals, initially using standardized test centers, then adopted remote BYOD‑style proctoring (Proctor Cam) as the method of choice within a year; the university reported a per‑student cost of more than $50 and strong perceived quality, despite student inconvenience</cite>. Although not a single exam, this illustrates BYOD‑style remote proctoring’s scalability to global cohorts and student acceptance.
- Research‑backed integrity parity: <cite id="8a3c840a-2">Experiments show un‑proctored BYOD can yield modest integrity losses (2.3% average score advantage vs. Zoom proctoring on non‑coding items), but adding question randomization more than doubles cheating gains when versions are identical (5.2% vs. 2.1%), supporting security‑by‑design for BYOD</cite>. <cite id="8a3c840a-1">There is no significant difference in performance between BYOD with Zoom proctoring and CBTC, suggesting comparable academic standards without BYOD’s capex</cite>.
- Large‑class BYOD feasibility: <cite id="2d98c357-3">A university course with several hundred students ran a BYOD programming exam; after a first‑time platform failure and some SEB (secure browser) launch issues, the team added backup submission via LMS journals, pre‑distributed config files, and “dummy” test USBs, which improved student confidence; the authors concluded benefits outweighed drawbacks</cite>. This documents practical steps for scaling BYOD exams and resolving technical bottlenecks before the final high‑stakes event.

Budgeting Playbook: Estimating Cost Per Student for BYOD vs. Rental Devices
- BYOD cost drivers:
  - Staffing: proctoring and operations. <cite id="8a3c840a-3">In‑person BYOD 20:1 and Zoom 40:1 ratios imply far fewer proctors than CBTC</cite>. <cite id="2d98c357-3">Add 10–20% contingency for technical support, backup devices, and mock‑test workshops to mitigate launch issues at scale</cite>.
  - IT infrastructure: <cite id="2d98c357-4">Bandwidth upgrades, heterogeneous device support, and classroom management add IT capex/Opex; if not already present, these can erode cost savings</cite>.
  - Software/Proctoring: <cite id="355fc501-2">Remote BYOD proctoring can add ~$50 per student if outsourced; in‑house Zoom proctoring can reduce per‑student cost but requires staff and monitoring capacity</cite>.
- Rental device cost drivers:
  - Device rental per unit + delivery/setup/collection. <cite id="8a3c840a-3">CBTC requires two proctors per room and overhead cameras (40–80 devices), implying significant labor and facility overhead per room</cite>.
  - Risk/Inventory: <cite id="2d98c357-4">Loss/theft/repair and bandwidth provisioning for many devices can add hidden costs</cite>.
Comparative rule of thumb: For >500 students, if the university can proctor BYOD with 20–40 students per proctor (in‑person/Zoom) and reuse existing classroom/lab space and IT staff, total cost per student is often lower than renting a device for each student plus staffing a CBTC or external centers. Where universities already invest in secure browser/online proctoring stacks, in‑house BYOD can approach or beat per‑student costs observed in remote programs (~$50) by leveraging internal proctoring staff and lab infrastructure. <cite id="8a3c840a-1">BYOD with Zoom proctoring yields results comparable to CBTC, supporting cost substitution of BYOD for CBTC</cite>. <cite id="355fc501-2">Remote BYOD proctoring at >$50 per student is feasible and acceptable, providing a benchmark for external rental‑plus‑proctoring arrangements</cite>.

Risks and Mitigations for BYOD in High‑Stakes Exams (>500 students)
Equity, device heterogeneity, and network constraints can undermine cost‑effectiveness if poorly managed. <cite id="2d98c357-4">BYOD can exacerbate equity gaps and classroom management challenges; IT infrastructure and bandwidth upgrades may be necessary, and the cost of upgrades can offset device savings</cite>. <cite id="2d98c357-3">Heterogeneous environments caused platform scalability limits and secure browser failures; pre‑testing with “dummy” config files, mock exams, and backup submission channels mitigated issues</cite>. <cite id="8a3c840a-2">Security risk is mitigated by combining proctoring with question randomization; un‑proctored BYOD shows a modest but real integrity risk, which increases without proctoring</cite>. For >500 students, plan for:
- Equity: device‑agnostic question design, offline‑capable exam packages, and loaner stock for critical cohorts.
- Readiness: mandatory pre‑exam self‑test environments, help desks, and staged rollouts.
- Supervision: adopt proven proctoring modalities (in‑person or remote) with documented ratios and monitoring protocols. <cite id="8a3c840a-3">Use 20–40 students per proctor ratios and camera review where feasible</cite>.
- Integrity: randomize questions/variants, use secure browsers, and log actions; consider un‑announced dry runs. <cite id="8a3c840a-2">Question randomization can halve cheating gains when versions are identical</cite>.

When BYOD Beats Rental Devices vs. When It Doesn’t
BYOD tends to be more cost‑effective when:
- The university already has sufficient invigilation staff, classroom/lab space, and network/IT capacity for large cohorts; BYOD reuses them across hundreds of students rather than provisioning new devices and rooms. <cite id="2d98c357-0">Dedicated CBTC centres are major cost centres, making BYOD more attractive</cite>. <cite id="8a3c840a-3">BYOD achieves comparable integrity with fewer proctors per student than CBTC</cite>.
- Proctoring software and secure browsing are already supported; BYOD leverages internal tools instead of paying per‑device rental fees. <cite id="355fc501-2">Remote proctoring at ~$50 per student is affordable if outsourced; in‑house can be cheaper</cite>.
BYOD tends to be less cost‑effective when:
- Infrastructure upgrades (bandwidth, device support, classroom management) are needed to accommodate heterogeneous devices at exam scale, eroding savings. <cite id="2d98c357-4">Cost savings are not automatic; infrastructure upgrades can outweigh device savings</cite>.
- Security/cheating risk requires heavier monitoring that exceeds the university’s capacity or budget. <cite id="8a3c840a-2">Unproctored BYOD shows a 2.3% average score advantage over Zoom proctoring on non‑coding items; without proctoring, risks escalate</cite>.

Practical Recommendations for >500‑Student Deployments
- Pilot at 100–200 students with BYOD, measure load on your LMS/secure browser, validate secure‑browser startup, and timebox technical support to refine operations before the main event. <cite id="2d98c357-3">Mock tests, config files, and backup plans resolved early‑exam failures in a hundreds‑scale run</cite>.
- Choose a proctoring strategy aligned to budget and risk: in‑person proctoring in classrooms (20:1) or remote Zoom proctoring (~40:1) with question randomization. <cite id="8a3c840a-3">Use staffing ratios to size proctor counts</cite>. <cite id="8a3c840a-2">Combine proctoring with question randomization to deter cheating, especially for non‑coding content</cite>.
- If remote BYOD proctoring is adopted, benchmark to known per‑student costs and negotiate pricing; if internal, avoid per‑student license costs by reusing existing proctoring infrastructure. <cite id="355fc501-2">> $50 per student is typical for outsourced remote proctoring; students accept the process</cite>.
- For rental devices, include per‑device rental fee, delivery/setup, technical support, and replacement budget; compare to BYOD’s per‑student proctoring budget plus IT/infrastructure upgrades. <cite id="8a3c840a-3">Labor and camera overhead per CBTC room are significant cost drivers</cite>. <cite id="2d98c357-4">Bandwidth and support capacity can add nontrivial Opex</cite>.
- Communicate and train: provide detailed pre‑exam checklists, tech support hotlines, and clear proctoring rules; use recorded demonstrations and help‑desk kiosks. <cite id="2d98c357-3">Providing dummy config files improved student confidence and familiarity</cite>.

Evidence Gaps and How to Resolve Them

Title: Securing Bring-Your-Own-Device (BYOD) Programming Exams
Snippet: In this section, we reflect on how effective our BYOD format was for the 2019 iteration of Digital World. We report on its advantages and disadvantages from three different perspectives. First, our own, as co-designers of the BYOD exam solution; second, those of our co-instructors who helped to run the exams; and third, those of our students, who were ultimately the ones subjected to it. Finally, we present our overall judgement as to whether the solution achieved our goals, and whether its benefits outweighed its drawbacks. 

Our Reflections. Our first use of the BYOD solution was in a onehour quiz taken by the entire cohort of students a few weeks before the mid-term. Despite conducting a mock test one week before this quiz, we ran into some difficulties that led to several improvements for subsequent exams. First, with several hundred students using the platform at the same time, Vocareum was not able to cope with the computational load, leading to several students being unable to submit or test their answers. We worked with Vocareum to address the root cause of the issue, and took steps to reassure students of this. We also devised new policies to mitigate any future technical issues with Vocareum, in particular, using Blackboard's native 'Assignment' and 'Journal' features as a backup means of submission. There were a small number of students who were not able to launch SEB at all during the quiz. They were provided with backup laptops during the test, and our Educational Technology department investigated afterwards. The most frequent reason for the problem was that the wrong version of SEB had been installed. We found that, despite organising a mock test, several students still struggled with SEB in the first quiz. To resolve this, we started providing 'dummy' SEB config files before the subsequent exams, which students could use to test the interface and practice programming within its restrictions. We observed that this improvement increased the students' confidence and familiarity with the exam environment. Related to this issue, the University of Tasmania (UTAS) reports that for their Linux USB BYOD exams, students are required to test the exam environment beforehand at an organised workshop or on their own [6].
</snippet>

Title: A South African university’s readiness assessment for bringing your own device for teaching and learning
Snippet: In an academic institution, security is not the main challenge but a critical concern to be considered. This is because it is difficult to monitor so many student mobile devices in one place (Hockly 2012). The following are some of the concerns for BYOD in education: 

• Equity -Traditionally, institutions provide learning technology to students, whereas BYOD allows students to bring their personally owned devices, creating an imbalance as some students cannot afford these devices. This causes more affluent students to have an unfair advantage over their classmates (Stavert 2013). • Classroom management -Effective classroom management is a requirement for effective education (Korpershoek et al. 2014). With many different mobile devices in one classroom, it is difficult to manage the proceedings in a classroom-based setting. • Not the best tool for the task -BYOD may not be the ideal technology for education regardless of the praise it gets; for example, a BYOD model that enables student's choice of device does not have personalised learning as its focus is not to provide each student with the best device for learning but rather whatever their families can afford (Dixon & Tierney 2012). • IT infrastructure and support -The challenge with moving from an 'already-in-place' technology to an 'unknown' one is the inadequacy of the IT infrastructure and support. • Bandwidth capacity -The worry with many mobile devices in one area attempting to all gain access to the network is bandwidth exhaustion (Mansfield-Devine 2012). • Cost -It is not clear whether BYOD reduces financial costs or not. However, some research studies argue that the objective of BYOD is not to save money (Sliep 2014); it should be about delivering education in new ways (Sweeney 2012). The reality is that even though BYOD sees institutions providing fewer technologies and devices for students, 'it does not ipso facto outweigh the cost for upgrading the IT infrastructure' (Sliep 2014). 

In order to successfully adopt and implement BYOD for education, there are countermeasures to address these concerns and they are discussed in the next section.

Title: Comparing the Security of Three Proctoring Regimens for Bring-Your-Own-Device Exams
Snippet: We compare the exam security of three proctoring regimens of Bring-Your-Own-Device, synchronous, computer-based exams in a computer science class: online un-proctored, online proctored via Zoom, and in-person proctored. We performed two randomized crossover experiments to compare these proctoring regimens. The first study measured the score advantage students receive while taking un-proctored online exams over Zoom-proctored online exams. The second study measured the score advantage of students taking Zoom-proctored online exams over in-person proctored exams. In both studies, students took six 50-minute exams using their own devices, which included two coding questions and 8--10 non-coding questions. We find that students score 2.3% higher on non-coding questions when taking exams in the un-proctored format compared to Zoom proctoring. No statistically significant advantage was found for the coding questions. While most of the non-coding questions had randomization such that students got different versions, for the few questions where all students received the same exact version, the score advantage escalated to 5.2%. From the second study, we find no statistically significant difference between students' performance on Zoom-proctored vs. in-person proctored exams. With this, we recommend educators incorporate some form of proctoring along with question randomization to mitigate cheating concerns in BYOD exams.
</snippet>

Title: Developing and teaching of a world-class online project management curriculum
Snippet: When we started the MS PM online program, the faculty unanimously decided to enforce the idea that all courses must have a proctored final examination. This was not common practice at the time, and the Office of Distance Education was at a loss as to how to implement the proctoring of exams for students all over the world. 

We were determined to find a solution, and for very good reasons: we wanted to ensure that the student in the course was indeed the student taking the exam; in other words, that the student was legitimate. Proctoring ensures such a validation as the student has to present a photo ID (such as a university ID, passport, or driver's licence) at the examination centre. Also, if the exams are closed book, the proctoring centre ensures that the student brings in no materials. 

Initially, most students took their proctored exams at standardised test centres. In special circumstances (e.g., military students overseas), we also allowed students to designate someone responsible (e.g., a senior military officer) as their proctor. The Office of Distance Education now has a dedicated staff member to help with finding proctoring centres and validating individual proctors. 

A new product called Procter Cam has emerged, which makes proctoring so much more convenient for everyone. By all accounts, Proctor Cam is a success and is working well. Proctor Cam allows the student to take the exam at their own computer, monitored by their own web camera. Proctoring is handled remotely by a live proctor: the student pans the camera around to ensure the exam conditions are proper; during the exam, the proctor monitors the student's desk and room to ensure no one comes in or talks to the student. 

Within a year of its introduction, Proctor Cam has become the method of choice for the majority of students. The cost of proctoring is substantial, more than $50 per student. However, this investment in proctoring, which is borne by the university not the students, is clearly correlated with quality, and this is evident even to students. We recall a memorable interaction in a water cooler discussion. A student was lamenting the trouble that he had to go through … driving to a proctoring centre and taking the exam. Another student remarked, "I'm in favour of going through this small inconvenience.
</snippet>

Snippet: In this paper, we perform, to our knowledge, the first controlled crossover experiment to (1) compare the security of three different proctoring regimens (un-proctored, Zoom proctoring, and inperson proctoring) for bring-your-own-device (BYOD) computerbased exams and (2) investigate the influence of question type, question randomization and proctoring on cheating in BYOD exams.

Based on our findings, we advocate the use of some form of proctoring over no proctoring at all.We find that students score 2.3 percentage points higher on average when un-proctored relative to Zoom proctored and that students perform similarly under Zoom proctoring and in-person proctoring.While the effect size of cheating in un-proctored exams is "modest" (0.116), we urge faculty to not discount it, as it is likely not uniformly distributed.Our experience suggests that cheating attempts are concentrated in a subset of students, for whom it would have a larger effect size.

In addition, we find additional evidence that question randomization is effective in deterring cheating.We find that the score advantage more than doubles (5.2 vs. 2.1 percentage points) for non-coding questions when all students receive the same version of the question.We suggest that faculty should use question randomization in any context where they are not 100% confident that cheating is negligible.

Summary
For large high‑stakes university exams (500+ students), the literature supports BYOD as a cost‑effective alternative to rental devices when institutions can maintain adequate IT infrastructure and robust proctoring/monitoring, because it avoids upfront device purchase and long‑term maintenance for a one‑off exam event and can leverage existing university resources rather than hiring and equipping external invigilators per student device. <cite id="2d98c357-0">When a dedicated wired‑computer exam centre is built and run, many BYOD limitations are eliminated but the setup and running costs are a major roadblock, making BYOD the economically viable option by comparison</cite>. <cite id="8a3c840a-0">A randomized study finds no performance advantage for students taking BYOD exams with Zoom proctoring versus computer‑based testing in a university lab (CBTC), indicating that BYOD proctored exams can sustain academic standards comparable to lab‑based proctored exams</cite>. <cite id="355fc501-2">A university online program reported a BYOD‑style remote proctoring success with per‑student proctoring cost of $50 and students preferring the convenience despite “small inconvenience,” supporting feasibility and student acceptance at scale</cite>.

Mechanisms of Cost‑Effectiveness
BYOD shifts capital and fleet‑management burden from the university to students while avoiding recurring rental fees and logistics (delivery, setup, collection, repair) for exam devices. <cite id="2d98c357-4">Readiness studies caution that BYOD’s cost savings are not guaranteed because institutions may avoid buying devices but must upgrade IT infrastructure and support to handle many heterogeneous devices; bandwidth and classroom management become major costs</cite>. <cite id="2d98c357-0">Institutions often find that building and operating a computer‑based testing (CBTC) centre with wired, centrally provisioned computers is capital‑ and OPEX‑intensive, whereas BYOD uses existing student devices and university networks to sidestep some capex and staffing costs, though security and supervision remain critical</cite>. <cite id="8a3c840a-3">Operational comparisons show BYOD can be run synchronously at class time with 20:1 student‑to‑proctor in classrooms and 40:1 with Zoom, while CBTC runs asynchronously with two proctors per room and camera review; these staffing cost structures inform relative labor cost profiles</cite>.

Implementation Comparisons for High‑Stakes Exams (>500 students)
Proctoring and supervision levels are decisive for cost and integrity outcomes. <cite id="8a3c840a-2">A controlled crossover experiment found students scored 2.3% higher on non‑coding questions in un‑proctored BYOD exams vs. Zoom‑proctored, with no significant advantage for coding; when versions were non‑randomized and identical, the advantage rose to 5.2%, and adding question randomization mitigates cheating risk</cite>. <cite id="8a3c840a-1">Across BYOD vs. Zoom vs. in‑person proctoring, differences in exam performance were not statistically significant, suggesting BYOD with appropriate proctoring preserves exam integrity comparable to other modes</cite>. <cite id="8a3c840a-4">Students scored about 1.5 percentage points lower on Zoom‑BYOD vs. in‑person proctored exams, but the difference was not statistically significant, reinforcing that with proctoring, BYOD can match in‑person integrity</cite>. <cite id="2d98c357-3">A multi‑hundred‑student BYOD programming exam revealed operational challenges under peak load (coding platform scalability, browser security blocker failures, some students unable to launch the secure exam browser), resolved via backup submission channels, pre‑exam “dummy” configuration files, and coordinated IT support; the authors judged benefits to outweigh drawbacks with proper preparation</cite>. These findings support a cost‑effective BYOD deployment when the university invests in pre‑exam readiness, monitoring, and rapid technical support.

Proctoring Cost Benchmarks and Staffing Ratios
Head‑to‑head staffing cost structures differ materially between BYOD and CBTC. <cite id="8a3c840a-3">BYOD in‑person proctoring used 20:1 ratios, Zoom proctoring used ~40:1, while CBTC used two proctors per room for 40–80 devices plus post‑exam camera review; CBTC also required dedicated staff per room and continuous camera oversight</cite>. <cite id="355fc501-2">In a programmatic rollout, remote BYOD‑style proctoring via Proctor Cam became the majority modality within a year, with a per‑student proctoring cost of more than $50 borne by the university and strong student acceptance despite the inconvenience, indicating that BYOD‑aligned remote proctoring can be both affordable and scalable</cite>. In contrast, rental device programs typically incur per‑device rental fees, delivery and setup labor, and inventory risk; the literature does not provide a single rental per‑device price, but the staffing and supervision costs above imply that BYOD can be lower total cost when the university can reuse staff and infrastructure across many students rather than provisioning and staffing a CBTC or external centers for each device.

Success Stories and Scale
- Online program proctoring success: <cite id="355fc501-2">An MS Program in Project Management mandated proctored finals, initially using standardized test centers, then adopted remote BYOD‑style proctoring (Proctor Cam) as the method of choice within a year; the university reported a per‑student cost of more than $50 and strong perceived quality, despite student inconvenience</cite>. Although not a single exam, this illustrates BYOD‑style remote proctoring’s scalability to global cohorts and student acceptance.
- Research‑backed integrity parity: <cite id="8a3c840a-2">Experiments show un‑proctored BYOD can yield modest integrity losses (2.3% average score advantage vs. Zoom proctoring on non‑coding items), but adding question randomization more than doubles cheating gains when versions are identical (5.2% vs. 2.1%), supporting security‑by‑design for BYOD</cite>. <cite id="8a3c840a-1">There is no significant difference in performance between BYOD with Zoom proctoring and CBTC, suggesting comparable academic standards without BYOD’s capex</cite>.
- Large‑class BYOD feasibility: <cite id="2d98c357-3">A university course with several hundred students ran a BYOD programming exam; after a first‑time platform failure and some SEB (secure browser) launch issues, the team added backup submission via LMS journals, pre‑distributed config files, and “dummy” test USBs, which improved student confidence; the authors concluded benefits outweighed drawbacks</cite>. This documents practical steps for scaling BYOD exams and resolving technical bottlenecks before the final high‑stakes event.

Budgeting Playbook: Estimating Cost Per Student for BYOD vs. Rental Devices
- BYOD cost drivers:
  - Staffing: proctoring and operations. <cite id="8a3c840a-3">In‑person BYOD 20:1 and Zoom 40:1 ratios imply far fewer proctors than CBTC</cite>. <cite id="2d98c357-3">Add 10–20% contingency for technical support, backup devices, and mock‑test workshops to mitigate launch issues at scale</cite>.
  - IT infrastructure: <cite id="2d98c357-4">Bandwidth upgrades, heterogeneous device support, and classroom management add IT capex/Opex; if not already present, these can erode cost savings</cite>.
  - Software/Proctoring: <cite id="355fc501-2">Remote BYOD proctoring can add ~$50 per student if outsourced; in‑house Zoom proctoring can reduce per‑student cost but requires staff and monitoring capacity</cite>.
- Rental device cost drivers:
  - Device rental per unit + delivery/setup/collection. <cite id="8a3c840a-3">CBTC requires two proctors per room and overhead cameras (40–80 devices), implying significant labor and facility overhead per room</cite>.
  - Risk/Inventory: <cite id="2d98c357-4">Loss/theft/repair and bandwidth provisioning for many devices can add hidden costs</cite>.
Comparative rule of thumb: For >500 students, if the university can proctor BYOD with 20–40 students per proctor (in‑person/Zoom) and reuse existing classroom/lab space and IT staff, total cost per student is often lower than renting a device for each student plus staffing a CBTC or external centers. Where universities already invest in secure browser/online proctoring stacks, in‑house BYOD can approach or beat per‑student costs observed in remote programs (~$50) by leveraging internal proctoring staff and lab infrastructure. <cite id="8a3c840a-1">BYOD with Zoom proctoring yields results comparable to CBTC, supporting cost substitution of BYOD for CBTC</cite>. <cite id="355fc501-2">Remote BYOD proctoring at >$50 per student is feasible and acceptable, providing a benchmark for external rental‑plus‑proctoring arrangements</cite>.

Risks and Mitigations for BYOD in High‑Stakes Exams (>500 students)
Equity, device heterogeneity, and network constraints can undermine cost‑effectiveness if poorly managed. <cite id="2d98c357-4">BYOD can exacerbate equity gaps and classroom management challenges; IT infrastructure and bandwidth upgrades may be necessary, and the cost of upgrades can offset device savings</cite>. <cite id="2d98c357-3">Heterogeneous environments caused platform scalability limits and secure browser failures; pre‑testing with “dummy” config files, mock exams, and backup submission channels mitigated issues</cite>. <cite id="8a3c840a-2">Security risk is mitigated by combining proctoring with question randomization; un‑proctored BYOD shows a modest but real integrity risk, which increases without proctoring</cite>. For >500 students, plan for:
- Equity: device‑agnostic question design, offline‑capable exam packages, and loaner stock for critical cohorts.
- Readiness: mandatory pre‑exam self‑test environments, help desks, and staged rollouts.
- Supervision: adopt proven proctoring modalities (in‑person or remote) with documented ratios and monitoring protocols. <cite id="8a3c840a-3">Use 20–40 students per proctor ratios and camera review where feasible</cite>.
- Integrity: randomize questions/variants, use secure browsers, and log actions; consider un‑announced dry runs. <cite id="8a3c840a-2">Question randomization can halve cheating gains when versions are identical</cite>.

When BYOD Beats Rental Devices vs. When It Doesn’t
BYOD tends to be more cost‑effective when:
- The university already has sufficient invigilation staff, classroom/lab space, and network/IT capacity for large cohorts; BYOD reuses them across hundreds of students rather than provisioning new devices and rooms. <cite id="2d98c357-0">Dedicated CBTC centres are major cost centres, making BYOD more attractive</cite>. <cite id="8a3c840a-3">BYOD achieves comparable integrity with fewer proctors per student than CBTC</cite>.
- Proctoring software and secure browsing are already supported; BYOD leverages internal tools instead of paying per‑device rental fees. <cite id="355fc501-2">Remote proctoring at ~$50 per student is affordable if outsourced; in‑house can be cheaper</cite>.
BYOD tends to be less cost‑effective when:
- Infrastructure upgrades (bandwidth, device support, classroom management) are needed to accommodate heterogeneous devices at exam scale, eroding savings. <cite id="2d98c357-4">Cost savings are not automatic; infrastructure upgrades can outweigh device savings</cite>.
- Security/cheating risk requires heavier monitoring that exceeds the university’s capacity or budget. <cite id="8a3c840a-2">Unproctored BYOD shows a 2.3% average score advantage over Zoom proctoring on non‑coding items; without proctoring, risks escalate</cite>.

Practical Recommendations for >500‑Student Deployments
- Pilot at 100–200 students with BYOD, measure load on your LMS/secure browser, validate secure‑browser startup, and timebox technical support to refine operations before the main event. <cite id="2d98c357-3">Mock tests, config files, and backup plans resolved early‑exam failures in a hundreds‑scale run</cite>.
- Choose a proctoring strategy aligned to budget and risk: in‑person proctoring in classrooms (20:1) or remote Zoom proctoring (~40:1) with question randomization. <cite id="8a3c840a-3">Use staffing ratios to size proctor counts</cite>. <cite id="8a3c840a-2">Combine proctoring with question randomization to deter cheating, especially for non‑coding content</cite>.
- If remote BYOD proctoring is adopted, benchmark to known per‑student costs and negotiate pricing; if internal, avoid per‑student license costs by reusing existing proctoring infrastructure. <cite id="355fc501-2">> $50 per student is typical for outsourced remote proctoring; students accept the process</cite>.
- For rental devices, include per‑device rental fee, delivery/setup, technical support, and replacement budget; compare to BYOD’s per‑student proctoring budget plus IT/infrastructure upgrades. <cite id="8a3c840a-3">Labor and camera overhead per CBTC room are significant cost drivers</cite>. <cite id="2d98c357-4">Bandwidth and support capacity can add nontrivial Opex</cite>.
- Communicate and train: provide detailed pre‑exam checklists, tech support hotlines, and clear proctoring rules; use recorded demonstrations and help‑desk kiosks. <cite id="2d98c357-3">Providing dummy config files improved student confidence and familiarity</cite>.

Evidence Gaps and How to Resolve Them
Peer‑reviewed studies provide strong evidence that BYOD can preserve exam integrity with appropriate proctoring and that large‑class BYOD operations are feasible with targeted mitigations, but they do not furnish rental device per‑device cost tables or university capex sheets for CBTC fleets. <cite id="8a3c840a-0">BYOD vs. CBTC performance equivalence</cite>, <cite id="8a3c840a-2">proctoring effectiveness and cheating mitigation via randomization</cite>, and <cite id="2d98c357-3">operational lessons from hundreds of students</cite> support cost‑effectiveness reasoning. Universities planning >500‑student exams should run a cost‑impact analysis that overlays their local rental rates and CBTC staffing/room costs with BYOD’s proctoring and infrastructure upgrade costs, and pilot with a representative cohort to validate network, device, and proctoring readiness before scale. <cite id="2d98c357-0">When CBTC setup/running costs are high, BYOD becomes the economically viable option</cite>, but <cite id="2d98c357-4">equity, bandwidth, and support capacity must be addressed to realize savings</cite>.

Bottom Line
For large, high‑stakes university exams, BYOD can be more cost‑effective than rental devices when institutions invest in proctoring, classroom/IT readiness, and device‑agnostic exam design. <cite id="8a3c840a-1">BYOD with Zoom proctoring performs equivalently to lab‑based proctored exams</cite>, and <cite id="355fc501-2">universities have deployed BYOD‑style remote proctoring at scale with per‑student costs around $50 and high student acceptance</cite>. <cite id="2d98c357-0">Where building and operating a CBTC centre is a major cost centre, shifting to BYOD can yield net savings by reusing staff and infrastructure, provided</cite> <cite id="2d98c357-4">equity, bandwidth, and support upgrades are planned and budgeted</cite> and <cite id="8a3c840a-2">proctoring plus question randomization is implemented to manage cheating risk</cite>. </answer>

Title: Students’ perceptions of BYOD open-book examinations in a large class
Snippet: Considering the increasing prevalence of tablets, one of the possible next steps should include the use of tablets as one of the devices in a BYOD e-exam. Currently, the use of tablets is still not possible due to security issues, especially in a high-stakes exam. However, it is understood that there are e-exam software companies who are developing the necessary apps for a BYOD e-exam on tablets. 

One common thread that runs through the areas for improvement is related to the exam venue, which ideally could be solved with a dedicated exam centre that is equipped with wired internet connected computers and that is large enough to accommodate a large class. With that, many of the limitations of a BYOD exam discussed in this paper will be eliminated, and the whole subject of a BYOD exam will not even surface. While the university is not discounting this option, the cost of setting-up and running such an exam centre remains as a major roadblock. Going forward, a BYOD e-exam, and all its associated limitations may be the only feasible and economically-viable option.

Title: The "Bring your own device" conundrum for organizations and investigators: An examination of the policy and legal concerns in light of investigatory challenges
Snippet: delays many policies and regulations attempt to address some of the latest developments and trends; however a litany of other issues are created in the process. One such issue is the use of personal BYOD implementations in the corporate environment instead of utilizing corporate owned devices. The corporate environment is making the BYOD shift due to the realized cost savings; however, a comprehensive cost benefit analysis must consider and account for all of the regulatory/policy issues and investigatory pitfalls that ultimately will arise from the use of the personally owned smartphones and other devices within enterprise. 

In this paper, the authors start with an overview of technologies normally included with the BYOD framework, and then move into the advantages of disadvantages organizations of BYOD initiatives. The authors examine relevant prior implementations noting benefits and drawbacks. In the next section, relevant laws and their organization impact are discussed, looking at established cases that may set precedent that organizations should consider along with some mitigation and handling techniques for the digital forensic examiner (hereinafter referred to as "DFE") for navigating in the realm of BYOD and corporate structure. Following that section, various mitigation techniques are discussed and addresses including both technical and administrative aspects.

Title: Securing Bring-Your-Own-Device (BYOD) Programming Exams
Snippet: In this section, we reflect on how effective our BYOD format was for the 2019 iteration of Digital World. We report on its advantages and disadvantages from three different perspectives. First, our own, as co-designers of the BYOD exam solution; second, those of our co-instructors who helped to run the exams; and third, those of our students, who were ultimately the ones subjected to it. Finally, we present our overall judgement as to whether the solution achieved our goals, and whether its benefits outweighed its drawbacks. 

Our Reflections. Our first use of the BYOD solution was in a onehour quiz taken by the entire cohort of students a few weeks before the mid-term. Despite conducting a mock test one week before this quiz, we ran into some difficulties that led to several improvements for subsequent exams. First, with several hundred students using the platform at the same time, Vocareum was not able to cope with the computational load, leading to several students being unable to submit or test their answers. We worked with Vocareum to address the root cause of the issue, and took steps to reassure students of this. We also devised new policies to mitigate any future technical issues with Vocareum, in particular, using Blackboard's native 'Assignment' and 'Journal' features as a backup means of submission. There were a small number of students who were not able to launch SEB at all during the quiz. They were provided with backup laptops during the test, and our Educational Technology department investigated afterwards. The most frequent reason for the problem was that the wrong version of SEB had been installed. We found that, despite organising a mock test, several students still struggled with SEB in the first quiz. To resolve this, we started providing 'dummy' SEB config files before the subsequent exams, which students could use to test the interface and practice programming within its restrictions. We observed that this improvement increased the students' confidence and familiarity with the exam environment. Related to this issue, the University of Tasmania (UTAS) reports that for their Linux USB BYOD exams, students are required to test the exam environment beforehand at an organised workshop or on their own [6].

Title: A South African university’s readiness assessment for bringing your own device for teaching and learning
Snippet: In an academic institution, security is not the main challenge but a critical concern to be considered. This is because it is difficult to monitor so many student mobile devices in one place (Hockly 2012). The following are some of the concerns for BYOD in education: 

• Equity -Traditionally, institutions provide learning technology to students, whereas BYOD allows students to bring their personally owned devices, creating an imbalance as some students cannot afford these devices. This causes more affluent students to have an unfair advantage over their classmates (Stavert 2013). • Classroom management -Effective classroom management is a requirement for effective education (Korpershoek et al. 2014). With many different mobile devices in one classroom, it is difficult to manage the proceedings in a classroom-based setting. • Not the best tool for the task -BYOD may not be the ideal technology for education regardless of the praise it gets; for example, a BYOD model that enables student's choice of device does not have personalised learning as its focus is not to provide each student with the best device for learning but rather whatever their families can afford (Dixon & Tierney 2012). • IT infrastructure and support -The challenge with moving from an 'already-in-place' technology to an 'unknown' one is the inadequacy of the IT infrastructure and support. • Bandwidth capacity -The worry with many mobile devices in one area attempting to all gain access to the network is bandwidth exhaustion (Mansfield-Devine 2012). • Cost -It is not clear whether BYOD reduces financial costs or not. However, some research studies argue that the objective of BYOD is not to save money (Sliep 2014); it should be about delivering education in new ways (Sweeney 2012). The reality is that even though BYOD sees institutions providing fewer technologies and devices for students, 'it does not ipso facto outweigh the cost for upgrading the IT infrastructure' (Sliep 2014). 

In order to successfully adopt and implement BYOD for education, there are countermeasures to address these concerns and they are discussed in the next section.

Title: Developing and teaching of a world-class online project management curriculum
Snippet: When we started the MS PM online program, the faculty unanimously decided to enforce the idea that all courses must have a proctored final examination. This was not common practice at the time, and the Office of Distance Education was at a loss as to how to implement the proctoring of exams for students all over the world. 

We were determined to find a solution, and for very good reasons: we wanted to ensure that the student in the course was indeed the student taking the exam; in other words, that the student was legitimate. Proctoring ensures such a validation as the student has to present a photo ID (such as a university ID, passport, or driver's licence) at the examination centre. Also, if the exams are closed book, the proctoring centre ensures that the student brings in no materials. 

Initially, most students took their proctored exams at standardised test centres. In special circumstances (e.g., military students overseas), we also allowed students to designate someone responsible (e.g., a senior military officer) as their proctor. The Office of Distance Education now has a dedicated staff member to help with finding proctoring centres and validating individual proctors. 

A new product called Procter Cam has emerged, which makes proctoring so much more convenient for everyone. By all accounts, Proctor Cam is a success and is working well. Proctor Cam allows the student to take the exam at their own computer, monitored by their own web camera. Proctoring is handled remotely by a live proctor: the student pans the camera around to ensure the exam conditions are proper; during the exam, the proctor monitors the student's desk and room to ensure no one comes in or talks to the student. 

Within a year of its introduction, Proctor Cam has become the method of choice for the majority of students. The cost of proctoring is substantial, more than $50 per student. However, this investment in proctoring, which is borne by the university not the students, is clearly correlated with quality, and this is evident even to students. We recall a memorable interaction in a water cooler discussion. A student was lamenting the trouble that he had to go through … driving to a proctoring centre and taking the exam. Another student remarked, "I'm in favour of going through this small inconvenience.

The first study measured the score advantage students receive while taking un-proctored online exams over Zoom-proctored online exams. In both studies, students took six 50-minute exams using their own devices, which included two coding questions and 8--10 non-coding questions. We find that students score 2.3% higher on non-coding questions when taking exams in the un-proctored format compared to Zoom proctoring. No statistically significant advantage was found for the coding questions. While most of the non-coding questions had randomization such that students got different versions, for the few questions where all students received the same exact version, the score advantage escalated to 5.2%. From the second study, we find no statistically significant difference between students' performance on Zoom-proctored vs. in-person proctored exams. Title: Comparing the Security of Three Proctoring Regimens for Bring-Your-Own-Device Exams
Snippet: In this paper, we perform, to our knowledge, the first controlled crossover experiment to (1) compare the security of three different proctoring regimens (un-proctored, Zoom proctoring, and inperson proctoring) for bring-your-own-device (BYOD) computerbased exams and (2) investigate the influence of question type, question randomization and proctoring on cheating in BYOD exams.

Based on our findings, we advocate the use of some form of proctoring over no proctoring at all.We find that students score 2.3 percentage points higher on average when un-proctored relative to Zoom proctored and that students perform similarly under Zoom proctoring and in-person proctoring.While the effect size of cheating in un-proctored exams is "modest" (0.116), we urge faculty to not discount it, as it is likely not uniformly distributed.Our experience suggests that cheating attempts are concentrated in a subset of students, for whom it would have a larger effect size.

In addition, we find additional evidence that question randomization is effective in deterring cheating.We find that the score advantage more than doubles (5.2 vs. 2.1 percentage points) for non-coding questions when all students receive the same version of the question.We suggest that faculty should use question randomization in any context where they are not 100% confident that cheating is negligible.

In addition, we find additional evidence that question randomization is effective in deterring cheating.We find that the score advantage more than doubles (5.2 vs. 2.1 percentage points) for non-coding questions when all students receive the same version of the question.We suggest that faculty should use question randomization in any context where they are not 100% confident that cheating is negligible.

documents.title: Developing and teaching of a world-class online project management curriculum
documents.snippet:
When we started the MS PM online program, the faculty unanimously decided to enforce the idea that all courses must have a proctored final examination. This was not common practice at the time, and the Office of Distance Education was at a loss as to how to implement the proctoring of exams for students all over the world. 

We were determined to find a solution, and for very good reasons: we wanted to ensure that the student in the course was indeed the student taking the exam; in other words, that the student was legitimate. Proctoring ensures such a validation as the student has to present a photo ID (such as a university ID, passport, or driver's licence) at the examination centre. Also, if the exams are closed book, the proctoring centre ensures that the student brings in no materials. 

Initially, most students took their proctored exams at standardised test centres. In special circumstances (e.g., military students overseas), we also allowed students to designate someone responsible (e.g., a senior military officer) as their proctor. The Office of Distance Education now has a dedicated staff member to help with finding proctoring centres and validating individual proctors. 

A new product called Procter Cam has emerged, which makes proctoring so much more convenient for everyone. By all accounts, Proctor Cam is a success and is working well. Proctor Cam allows the student to take the exam at their own computer, monitored by their own web camera. Proctoring is handled remotely by a live proctor: the student pans the camera around to ensure the exam conditions are proper; during the exam, the proctor monitors the student's desk and room to ensure no one comes in or talks to the student. 

Within a year of its introduction, Proctor Cam has become the method of choice for the majority of students. The cost of proctoring is substantial, more than $50 per student. However, this investment in proctoring, which is borne by the university not the students, is clearly correlated with quality, and this is evident even to students. We recall a memorable interaction in a water cooler discussion. A student was lamenting the trouble that he had to go through … driving to a proctoring centre and taking the exam. Another student remarked, "I'm in favour of going through this small inconvenience.

documents.title: Comparing the Security of Three Proctoring Regimens for Bring-Your-Own-Device Exams
documents.snippet: We compare the exam security of three proctoring regimens of Bring-Your-Own-Device, synchronous, computer-based exams in a computer science class: online un-proctored, online proctored via Zoom, and in-person proctored. We performed two randomized crossover experiments to compare these proctoring regimens. The first study measured the score advantage students receive while taking un-proctored online exams over Zoom-proctored online exams. The second study measured the score advantage of students taking Zoom-proctored online exams over in-person proctored exams. In both studies, students took six 50-minute exams using their own devices, which included two coding questions and 8--10 non-coding questions. We find that students score 2.3% higher on non-coding questions when taking exams in the un-proctored format compared to Zoom proctoring. No statistically significant advantage was found for the coding questions. While most of the non-coding questions had randomization such that students got different versions, for the few questions where all students received the same exact version, the score advantage escalated to 5.2%. From the second study, we find no statistically significant difference between students' performance on Zoom-proctored vs. in-person proctored exams. With this, we recommend educators incorporate some form of proctoring along with question randomization to mitigate cheating concerns in BYOD exams.
